entry.heading: Blue Lock
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Find what only you can do and pursue it without apology. Hunger to win, honest self-analysis and constant adaptation make you great. Others are rivals to learn from and "devour," and teamwork is valuable when it serves the strongest individual.

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; recurring inside

frames.aligns: Excellence and use of one's gifts (the parable of the talents); perseverance; honest self-examination; Kuon's betrayal framed as wrong and followed by effort to make amends.
frames.concerns: The story teaches self-assertion over solidarity and treats others as tools ("devour" them); pride is a capital sin, and the Church's media documents ask that media serve human dignity and the common good. Frequent f-words and "goddamn" in the dialogue.

frames.aligns: Discipline and ascetic-like training; facing one's weaknesses honestly.
frames.concerns: The Fathers count pride and vainglory among the most dangerous passions, and the story makes them the engine of growth. Watchfulness (nepsis) asks what a steady diet of "monster ego" imagery forms in a young reader.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-discipline, using gifts fully; cheating shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Philippians 2:3 ("Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit") runs directly against the story's thesis. Frequent f-words and "goddamn" (Ephesians 4:29; the Third Commandment). Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, excellence "as working for the Lord" (Colossians 3:23), learning from failure.
frames.concerns: Selfish ambition presented as the virtue; others treated as stepping stones. Many evangelicals distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it; here the story endorses ego, so it is a message issue. Profanity.

frames.aligns: Boldness, confidence, refusing to be passive; discipline.
frames.concerns: Self-exaltation as the path to power; divine and royal titles for star players. No occult practice; the "Awakening" auras with flaming-eyed skulls, a Buddha quote and karma talk (Plugged In, film) are minor points some families may note. Profanity. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a well-made sports story by non-Christians; the story is honest about human ambition and rivalry.
frames.concerns: Self-glory as the chief end, against "man's chief end is to glorify God" (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q1).

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; vocation; honest admission of weakness and failure.
frames.concerns: Self-justification by performance runs against grace alone: worth in Blue Lock is earned by scoring, and losers are "trash." LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.
Wesley's question whether a diversion can be "used in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would weigh self-exaltation and profanity heavily; the United Methodist Church is much more open.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges how a story frames good and evil: here, cheating is wrong, honest effort is rewarded.
frames.concerns: The story frames pride as good and self-giving as weakness, the reverse of the tradition's framing. Practice ranges from progressive to conservative.

Humility and yieldedness to the community (Gelassenheit) and avoiding pride and worldliness are core; the story's message is the opposite, so this is a message issue, not only a depiction one. Old Order groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Self-improvement, hard work, setting high goals, accountability for choices.
frames.concerns: President Ezra Taft Benson's well-known 1989 talk "Beware of Pride" describes pride as enmity toward others and competition to be above them, close to the program's design (from general knowledge; to verify). For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit; profanity.

frames.aligns: Critique of conformity; diverse personalities given space to grow; foreign characters shown positively (Common Sense Media).
frames.concerns: A cutthroat system run on teenagers is shown as justified by results; losers are discarded; the vulnerable (eliminated players) vanish from the story.

frames.aligns: Discipline, healthy training, perseverance, no substances.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": constant celebration of self-exalting rivalry; Ellen White's writings warn against amusements that stir competitive passions (from general knowledge; to verify). Profanity.

frames.aligns: Honesty, discipline, avoiding substances and occult content.
frames.concerns: Witness publications counsel against a competitive spirit that makes a person want to be above others (Galatians 5:26, "not becoming egotistical, stirring up competition with one another"); the series makes that spirit the whole point (from general knowledge; to verify). Profanity.

frames.aligns: The power of thought and self-belief to change performance; overcoming fear; mental clarity (Isagi's analysis).
frames.concerns: The thought the story cultivates is self-centered and fear-driven (fear of elimination); "Stand porter at the door of thought" asks what fills the mind.

frames.aligns: Effort (hishtadlut) and honest self-assessment (cheshbon hanefesh); a rabbinic tradition that even the "evil inclination" drives people to build and achieve (Genesis Rabbah 9:7).
frames.concerns: Humility (anavah) is a central trait; Pirkei Avot 4:1 ("Who is honored? One who honors others") inverts the program's values. Harsh insults (onaat devarim). Many Haredi homes restrict secular media like this; Modern Orthodox families are selective.

frames.aligns: Ambition harnessed for growth (Genesis Rabbah 9:7); honest self-assessment; perseverance after failure.
frames.concerns: Humility and kind speech; others as tools.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; developing one's unique gifts; critique of blind conformity.
frames.concerns: Tikkun olam and the dignity of each person: the eliminated players are discarded.

frames.aligns: Striving for excellence (ihsan), discipline, honest effort, perseverance.
frames.concerns: Arrogance (kibr) is strongly condemned in the Qur'an and hadith; the story treats self-exaltation as virtue. Insults and profanity.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: finding one's own nature and role; disciplined action; intense focus (Isagi's "flow").
frames.concerns: The Gita teaches action without attachment to the fruits (2:47) and warns against ahamkara (ego); the story makes desire for victory and ego the fuel. Rajasic qualities (passion, rivalry) dominate.

frames.aligns: Right effort, concentration and honest self-observation; the "flow" state resembles absorption.
frames.concerns: The series explicitly cultivates ego and craving for victory, the roots of suffering in Buddhist teaching (Four Noble Truths; anatta, non-self); rivals are to be "devoured." This is a central message conflict, though nothing is graphic.

frames.aligns: Discipline, courage, standing up for oneself.
frames.concerns: Haumai (ego) is one of the five vices and the core obstacle to liberation; the frame guide notes concern when the five vices are "shown as admirable," and the story is built on admiring ego and anger.

frames.aligns: Excellence, developing one's capacities, unity across nations (foreign players shown positively).
frames.concerns: 'Abdu'l-Bahá taught that the "struggle for existence" is the source of conflict and that cooperation is the basis of human progress (from general knowledge; to verify); the story is a struggle for existence among teens.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) of effort; purity of dedication; national community.
frames.concerns: The story is an explicit critique of harmony (wa) and group belonging, values that shrine tradition expresses and reinforces; gratitude is rare. No disrespect to shrines or kami. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Personal will and empowerment, self-knowledge, transformation.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none"): the program harms players' futures; little reverence for nature. No portrayal of witches or pagans.

frames.aligns: Competence, self-determinism, personal survival (the first dynamic), discipline and training; no psychiatry content. The Way to Happiness precept "Be competent."
frames.concerns: The eight dynamics also include family, group and humankind; the story ranks the group dynamic below the self. The church's own materials say little about anime.

frames.aligns: Critique of conformity; foreign characters shown positively; some critique of the football establishment.
frames.concerns: At the message level, an extreme-competition, winner-take-all system run on minors is presented as admirable; critics read it as promoting hierarchy and hyper-competition (The Daily Campus). Almost no women.

frames.aligns: Self-determination, reason and analysis (Isagi wins by thinking), merit, critical view of tradition and authority.
frames.concerns: Cruelty toward youths (lifetime bans, humiliation) is justified by results; dignity of the eliminated players is ignored.

frames.aligns: Meritocracy, discipline, competition, excellence, national pride (the goal is a World Cup win for Japan), personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: The story rejects inherited institutions (the football establishment, team harmony, seniority) and puts self above duty.

frames.aligns: Free search for one's own path; critique of conformity.
frames.concerns: The inherent worth and dignity of every person versus a system that discards losers; the interdependent web versus "devour your rivals."

frames.aligns: The Church of Satan treats rational self-interest as a virtue, sees each person as their own god, rejects false humility and values the strong, self-made individual; Blue Lock's creed of ego, self-knowledge and "becoming the best" is close to this. Rejection of the conformist establishment fits both groups. (Range: Church of Satan near S; The Satanic Temple lower.)
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's tenets stress compassion, justice and the dignity of others; Kaiser's cruelty and the treatment of eliminated players would concern TST readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pride and the hunger to "devour" rivals are honored, and Rin's rage at Sae (ch. 115 onward) fuels his game. But disputes are settled on the pitch under the rules, and Kuon's cheating is condemned (First Selection, ch. 18-25).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates the individual striker over team harmony (Ego's founding speech, ch. 1-3). Ego himself is an authoritarian figure inside a locked facility, so freedom is pursued through a harsh, rule-bound program.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty goes neither to family nor clan: kin ties appear mostly as wounds (the Itoshi brothers) and friendship is secondary to ego (Nagi leaves Reo, Second Selection). The program's goal is a national team, not a family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank is everywhere (ranking screens, NEL bids, "emperor" and "god" titles, ch. 155 onward), but it is earned by results. Seniority and the football association's bureaucracy are critiqued.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith appears. Isagi grows through analysis, "formulas" and copying what works (Pragmatic lens). Traditional Japanese team harmony is presented as the cause of failure (ch. 1).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The life message is "find what only you can do and pursue it without apology," a strong self-expression value. The setting is a survival contest with lifetime bans for losers (ch. 1-3), which keeps it near the middle.

folkways.japan: The series is an argument with Japanese norms; Kaneshiro says frustration with Japanese society shaped the focus on ego. Team harmony (wa), seniority and self-effacement are the values it pushes against, so readers from more individualist cultures may find its "ego" less radical than Japanese readers do.

entry.dominant: Existentialism (self-creation), Expressive individualism, Pragmatism, Might makes right ("skill makes right"), Classical virtue ethics; Communitarianism and Confucian-style harmony critiqued.

entry.heading: Horimiya (HERO and Daisuke Hagiwara)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from being known and accepted as you really are by a few people who choose you, and from caring for them in daily, ordinary ways; loneliness is the thing to be rescued from.

frames.aligns: Self-giving care (Hori for Souta, Miyamura for everyone); dignity of the outcast; forgiveness; movement toward marriage and family.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex between teens treated as a natural step, not a moral question (CCC 2353 on fornication; 2337-2350 on chastity). Hori's hitting partly played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Humility, love shown in small daily service, healing of a wounded soul through communion with others.
frames.concerns: Premarital union outside the mystery of marriage; passions (anger, jealousy) played as cute. Guarding the senses applies mainly to the romance focus.

frames.aligns: Clear kindness, loyalty and forgiveness; care for siblings; marriage as the hoped-for end.
frames.concerns: Teen sex outside marriage endorsed by silence (1 Corinthians 6:18; Hebrews 13:4); dating culture with no adult guidance. Each congregation decides how strict to be.

frames.aligns: "Do not judge by appearances" (John 7:24) is the story's core; friends restore the lonely; apologies and reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex shown as normal and good; romance as the main source of meaning. Engage-or-separate views differ by family.

frames.aligns: Restoration of the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3 echo in Miyamura's arc); joy, warmth, community.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics; holiness standards on modesty and tattoos vary by church (Leviticus 19:28 read by some). No occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a kind, well-made story by non-Christians; honesty and confession of fault after fights (ch. 42).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists lascivious books among sins against the seventh commandment; ch. 37 and ch. 43 are the test cases, though nothing is shown. Teen sex is unchallenged.

frames.aligns: Vocation in daily life: Hori's household work, Miyamura's bakery, care for neighbors. Confession and forgiveness between friends.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment on sex before marriage. LCMS and WELS families tend to weigh ch. 37 more heavily than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and social holiness on a small scale; inclusion of the outsider.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex; Hori's violence partly comic. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Kindness, belonging and reconciliation framed as good; strong literary tradition of reading romance generously.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics, where Episcopal and ACNA families differ. Partner violence played lightly.

frames.aligns: Humility, simple daily service, peaceable friendship, forgiveness of a former bully (Tanihara).
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes a secular teen-romance series a concern for Old Order families; teen sex; Hori's violence. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family-centered life, caring for siblings, eventual marriage and a child (webcomic ending); kindness and ministering.
frames.concerns: Law of chastity: teen sex before marriage (ch. 37) shown without consequence. For the Strength of Youth also asks youth to treat the body as sacred (tattoos and piercings, read by many families as counsel to avoid).

frames.aligns: Welcome of the outsider, acceptance of a transgender character (CSM), gentle reversed gender roles, depression taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Partner violence by Hori sometimes a joke; tattoo appropriation (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Kindness, service, family care, the body healed of old harm.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex; tattoos and piercings run against counsel on adornment and body as temple. Entertainment centered on romance excites "the passions" in Ellen White's sense.
Dating as a teen with no marriage aim at first, and sex before marriage (ch. 37), both against jw.org counsel; Hori's violence. No spiritism.

frames.aligns: Love heals: Miyamura's loneliness and dark thoughts give way to affection and belonging, without medicine.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on past self-harm and sorrow; sexual relations outside marriage.

frames.aligns: Hesed (lovingkindness), honoring and caring for family, forgiveness, marriage and children as the hoped-for end.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen dating, implied sex, shirtless art; many Haredi homes would not have the series. Tattoos (Leviticus 19:28).

frames.aligns: Lovingkindness, dignity of every person, family responsibility.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics for teens; tattoos (Leviticus 19:28) discussed by families; Hori's violence.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person, inclusion, emotional honesty, a transgender character accepted (CSM).
frames.concerns: Partner violence played lightly; teen sex left to family values.

frames.aligns: Kindness, family duty (Hori and Souta), mercy toward a former bully, marriage as the goal.
frames.concerns: The premise is unchaperoned dating; sex before marriage (ch. 37) is presented as good (zina; Qur'an 17:32). Tattoos widely held impermissible. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for shirtless scenes.

frames.aligns: Seva and family dharma (Hori raising Souta, Miyamura's bakery), kindness to the excluded.
frames.concerns: Premarital relations conflict with brahmacharya for students; some families apply the Gita's categories to a romance-centered work.

frames.aligns: Compassion for suffering; loneliness and self-harm shown as suffering that ends through connection; right speech in apologies.
frames.concerns: Third precept (sexual misconduct) read differently across schools; attachment and jealousy (Hori) romanticized.

frames.aligns: Seva, honest work (Miyamura's bakery), compassion, forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) and krodh (anger) are among the five vices: Hori's anger is often a joke, and premarital sex is shown as good. Hair cutting and body modification run against the Khalsa ideal for observant families.

frames.aligns: Unity, service, kindness, inclusion of the outcast.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" makes sex before marriage (ch. 37) a clear conflict; parental consent to marriage is also a Bahá'í principle, while Hori's father is a joke.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude, harmony in the group; a New Year shrine visit shown naturally (vol. 10).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; tattoos carry social stigma in Japan, which the story treats as unfair.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" in kindness; acceptance of difference and body art; no stereotyping of pagans.
The Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, help and care for children (Souta), be faithful to one's partner; problems resolved by communication.
frames.concerns: Depression resolved without professional help fits the Church's opposition to psychiatry; Hori's violence.

frames.aligns: Anti-bullying, emotional honesty, accepted transgender character (CSM), reversed gender roles, mental health taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Partner violence by Hori sometimes a gag, and her wish for him to be "mean" (Girls in Capes); appropriated tribal tattoo designs and an anime-only teacher remark (Anime Feminist); self-harm not addressed with help-seeking.

frames.aligns: Human connection as the source of meaning; kindness and honesty without religious framing; a finite, ordinary life made good.
frames.concerns: Depression resolved by love alone, with no adult or professional help shown.

frames.aligns: Commitment, marriage and children as the goal; hard work and family business; caring for siblings; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Teen premarital sex unchallenged; tattoos and piercings; a comic, absent father; a girl who hits her boyfriend.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the outcast; acceptance of difference including a transgender character; healing through community.
Self-expression and refusing to conform to school appearance norms; consensual pleasure without guilt; loyalty to those who earn it (Church of Satan); compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Hori's violence breaks the bodily-autonomy tenet (Tenet 3); forgiving a bully may read as weakness to Church of Satan readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The story's core is the inner worth of a mocked boy, not reputation. But Hori defends his name with her fists against old classmates (ch. 38), and her outbursts are partly a defense of the couple's standing.

Order vs freedom.evidence: School rules on appearance are shown as something to work around: Miyamura hides tattoos in winter uniforms (TV Tropes). Friends and couples set their own terms with little adult oversight.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family duty matters (Hori and Souta; Miyamura's bakery; Iura's siblings), but the chosen friend group is the main circle of care.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Friends treat each other as equals across popularity lines; the student council and teachers have little standing; the father is mocked.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with customs kept lightly (New Year shrine, vol. 10); marriage and family business as the end.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being yourself and being accepted is the central value; body art and hidden selves are welcomed. Hard work at home is present but not the point.

folkways.japan: The stigma on tattoos (yakuza association), the strict school rules on appearance, senpai-kohai relations, the shrine visit at New Year and the expectation that a son will take over the family shop are Japanese norms that frame the story more than they form its message. The value of quiet acceptance within a close group also reflects Japanese school life.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Bleach
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent protecting the people you love, with your own heart as the guide even when authorities or gods are wrong; fear and death are part of life and give courage its meaning.

content.framing: Neutral (sword combat as the story's main action); Shown with consequences for atrocities

frames.aligns: Evil is shown but not made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7): Aizen's pride and Yhwach's tyranny fall. Self-giving love (Masaki dies shielding her son; Ukitake gives his life, ch. 616-617). Mercy toward defeated enemies.
frames.concerns: Sacred signs (crosses, a blood-drinking rite, God's name) used as villain costume; a "god" who is a sealed object; afterlife without God's judgment except a vague Hell. Aizen and Beneath the Tangles: the Satan-like figure who wants "the throne of heaven."

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Aizen's pride, Yhwach's will to power); Ichigo's humility and mercy.
frames.concerns: Holy images and the Cross are venerated, so crosses and a communion-like rite on the villains are a weighty matter; "death gods" and spirit traffic with the dead. Guarding the senses makes the gore itself a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear defeat of the prideful villains; loyalty and courage.
frames.concerns: Afterlife run by "death gods," reincarnation and an imprisoned "god" (John 14:6; Hebrews 9:27); villain named after God. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Aizen as a Satan figure defeated by a "Messiah-figure," Ichigo. Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife shown as real; misuse of God's name (Exodus 20:7) for a villain; Christian imagery on the aggressor army.

frames.aligns: Courage, protection of the weak, good overcoming evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": the whole premise is traffic with the dead, spirits, Hollows and death gods; Hell shown as a living force; God's name on a villain. Views vary widely by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows valuing good art by non-Christians; total depravity has an echo in Soul Society's own crimes (ch. 46, 124): no side is pure.
frames.concerns: Second commandment concerns about a "god" figure drawn and dismembered; misuse of God's name; spiritism premise.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Soul Society bears the sword, flawed but needed. Law and gospel: no one in the story is saved by their own merit alone.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife; sacred imagery for villains; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy: Ichigo protects ghosts and the weak; repentance possible (Byakuya, Renji change).
frames.concerns: Spiritism premise; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Strong fantasy tradition (Lewis, Sayers): good and evil judged by framing; just war fits Soul Society's defense.
frames.concerns: Use of crosses and a communion-like rite on the villains; God's name on a villain.

frames.aligns: Humility, mercy toward beaten enemies, distrust of state power (Central 46 wrong, ch. 46 extermination).
frames.concerns: Sword violence is the heroes' tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); a war epic.

frames.aligns: Life continues after death; family love and marriage (ch. 686); agency against tyranny.
frames.concerns: Afterlife structure differs from the plan of salvation; God's name on a villain; fan service.

frames.aligns: Critique of unjust institutions and of genocide by "good" powers (ch. 46); compassion for outsiders (Hollows as lost souls).
frames.concerns: Giselle as a trans-coded sadist (ANN; Anime Feminist); Nazi aesthetics used for spectacle; women sidelined.
The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so the entire premise (souls living on, death gods, Hell as a present place) conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.
Spiritism and contact with the dead are the premise; the cross as a sacred symbol (Witnesses reject it) and God's personal name (Jehovah, from YHWH) given to a villain; heroic violence.

frames.aligns: Ichigo and Aizen's last words both hold that fear can be faced; courage over fear.
frames.concerns: Death, Hollows and Hell shown as real and powerful; dwelling on fear and gore.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; condemnation of a tyrant who sacrifices his own people (ch. 603, 680); memory of a destroyed people as a plot force.
frames.concerns: The Tetragrammaton, which is not pronounced, adapted as the name of a villain who calls himself "The Almighty" (ch. 565; GameRant); SS-named guard and "selection" (Auswählen) used for spectacle; spirit contact with the dead. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; the Quincy's history of being wiped out (ch. 46) treated as a real wrong.
frames.concerns: God's name on a villain; Nazi-style aesthetics (ANN: "an overt nazi motif"); a "selection" that kills the weak and mixed-blood (ch. 537, 603).

frames.aligns: Critique of genocide and of blood-purity ideology (Echt versus Gemischt, ch. 531; Yhwach killing the "impure," ch. 537); tikkun olam echoes in protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Nazi-coded aesthetics without historical framing; the divine name for a villain; Giselle's trans-coded villainy.

frames.aligns: Justice against tyranny; mercy to defeated foes; patience under trial; the prideful seeker of godhood (Aizen) brought low.
frames.concerns: A supreme being depicted as a body, dismembered and killed (ch. 611-621); claimants to divinity ("The Almighty"); intermediaries controlling souls; lowering the gaze for fan service.

frames.aligns: Souls cycle between worlds and return to life; dharma of the warrior who protects; death gods echo Yama's servants.
frames.concerns: God-figure reduced to an object; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Hollows as souls trapped by attachment and despair; impermanence; a balance of souls; Aizen's and Yhwach's craving for supremacy undone.
frames.concerns: Killing is the main solution, against the first precept; the cosmology is a bureaucracy rather than a path to liberation.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier ideal: courage to defend the oppressed; ego (haumai) shown in Aizen and Yhwach and defeated.
frames.concerns: Little in message; heroic violence and a dismembered "god" may be discussed.

frames.aligns: Unity across peoples (Shinigami, Quincy, Arrancar fight together at the end); justice against tyranny.
frames.concerns: Commitment to non-violence; prejudice about blood purity is the villains' creed but still shown at length.

frames.aligns: Shinigami, konso purification, kami-like beings, spirits of the dead treated as part of the world; sincerity and loyalty in Ichigo.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity; a kami-like Soul King treated as a mechanism.

frames.aligns: Death as part of a cycle; spirits and the world of the dead treated as real and natural; no stereotyping of witches (Kubo's later series Burn the Witch is separate).
Souls survive death and return to new bodies, with an echo of the thetan idea; personal ability and will win. The Way to Happiness: help others, do not murder.
frames.concerns: Mayuri's experiments and drugging; killing as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Critique of corrupt institutions and of genocide; blood-purity ideology framed as villainous (ch. 531, 537).
frames.concerns: Giselle's trans-coded villainy (ANN: "left field transphobia"; Anime Feminist); Nemu's abuse played for comedy; women sidelined (Orihime, Momo, Rukia); Yumichika mocked; Nazi aesthetic as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Aizen's final reflection: a world without fear of death would lack the hope and courage that hold death off (fan wiki, Aizen page; likely ch. 685). Gods are exposed as power structures; human choices matter.
frames.concerns: Mayuri's cruelty played partly for fun; violence as the default answer.

frames.aligns: Protective masculinity, loyalty, honor, duty; family and marriage in the ending (ch. 686).
frames.concerns: The defining hero act is defying lawful authority (Soul Society's sentence on Rukia); the "god" at the top is a fraud; mixed respect for tradition.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of all souls, including Hollows; justice for the wronged (the Quincy); free search for truth about the gods.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; gender and queer portrayals (Giselle, Yumichika).

frames.aligns: Questioning gods and authority: Soul Society's law is wrong and the Soul King is a fraud; individual will and pride celebrated in fighters (Kenpachi, Grimmjow). Tenets on compassion and justice.
frames.concerns: The rebels against "heaven" (Aizen, Yhwach) are the villains and lose; harm to the weak by tyrants is condemned, as the tradition would too.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal pride and duels decide almost everything: Kenpachi, Byakuya's honor, Grimmjow's rivalry, captains defending their names. Ichigo's mercy toward beaten foes softens it.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The founding act is defying Soul Society's law to save Rukia (vols. 8-20); Central 46 is wrong and Soul Society's history hides crimes (ch. 46, 621). Order is restored, but conscience over rule is celebrated.

Civic vs kin.evidence: "I'll protect" family and friends is Ichigo's creed; Masaki's sacrifice; the Kuchiki choice between law and sister ends with kin winning.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Captains, lieutenants, numbered Espada and noble houses are central and respected, but rank is overturned by a teenager and noble privilege is shown critically.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The setting is spiritual, yet gods are exposed as structures (the Soul King "thing," ch. 421, 621) and science (Urahara, Mayuri) is powerful.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and survival dominate the last arc, while style, fashion and personal expression mark nearly every character.

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai and rank deference among Soul Reapers, the noble house as a Japanese aristocratic model, Shinto purification and Buddhist-style death rites, and high-school friendship groups are Japanese norms that frame the story; the German, Spanish and Christian elements are borrowed as style.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, a critique of Might makes right and of Collectivism/authoritarianism, with Dharmic and Shinto cosmology as setting. Labels other than those quoted from sources are our framing.

series.title: Kaguya-sama: Love is War
series.romaji: Kaguya-sama wa Kokurasetai: Tensaitachi no Renai Zunousen
series.native: かぐや様は告らせたい～天才たちの恋愛頭脳戦～

entry.heading: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life takes the courage to be honest and vulnerable. Pride, mind games and fear of rejection keep people lonely; friends who see the real you, and love freely chosen, are worth more than wealth, status or family control.

frames.aligns: Lies and manipulation are shown to fail; truthful, faithful love wins; justice for the falsely accused Ishigami; fidelity across distance.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex framed as a loving milestone (ch. 220) contrary to chastity teaching (CCC 2337-2359); recurring sex jokes and a porn DVD gag; resisting parents is justified by the family's coldness.

frames.aligns: Humility conquers pride, the "passion" the leads must overcome; friendship and forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex framed positively; sexual talk works against guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Honesty, hard work, faithfulness, care for an outcast (Ishigami).
frames.concerns: Premarital sex framed positively (ch. 220); sex jokes and the porn DVD joke fail the Philippians 4:8 test for many; deceptive heroes.

frames.aligns: Vulnerability and confession as the way to real love; redemption for the isolated; the story outgrows its scheming.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics of the later volumes; frequent crude humor.

frames.aligns: Little occult content; love, loyalty and courage.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex and sexual humor against holiness standards; fortune-telling gags (vol. 16).

frames.aligns: Common grace: a well-crafted story of pride humbled; truth-telling (ninth commandment) wins.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" and unchaste talk; ch. 220 endorses premarital sex.

frames.aligns: Adiaphora judged by love: the core message (honesty, mercy for Ishigami) fits; "put the best construction on everything" fits the forgiving tone. LCMS/WELS families will lean C.
frames.concerns: Sixth-commandment concerns about premarital sex (ch. 220) and sex jokes.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: friends caring for the outcast; growth in character. Holiness and Global Methodist families will lean C.
frames.concerns: Explicit-talk humor and the endorsed first night.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: cruelty (Ogino) and coldness are condemned, honesty rewarded. ACNA families will lean C.
Nonviolence mostly; humility over pride; community that restores the outcast.
frames.concerns: Worldly romance, wealth and status culture; premarital sex; sex humor. Old Order families would avoid it entirely.

frames.aligns: Honesty (Article of Faith 13), hard work, loyal friends, eventual implied marriage (an Oshi no Ko bonus chapter credits "Kaguya Shirogane").
frames.concerns: Law of chastity conflicts with ch. 220 and with the Kashiwagi couple; sexual jokes against For the Strength of Youth.

frames.aligns: Consent-based, caring relationship; critique of misogyny and family control; justice for the wrongly accused; class barriers overcome.
frames.concerns: Teasing manipulation in early chapters; some jokes about bodies; spying as comedy.
Ellen White's warnings about romance fiction that excites the passions; premarital sex; sexual talk.

frames.aligns: Little violence or spiritism; honesty and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) framed positively in ch. 220; sexual jokes.

frames.aligns: Low fear and disease content; healing comes through love and right thinking among friends; thought shapes experience, and the leads' anxious "mental battles" are shown as self-defeating.
frames.concerns: Purity and marriage valued; the endorsed first night and sexual talk.

frames.aligns: "Keep far from falsehood" (Exodus 23:7): the lies collapse; defending a wronged person; justice for Ishigami.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: sexual talk, a porn DVD joke, a teen couple's first night; nivul peh (crude speech).

frames.aligns: Kind speech, dignity, justice for the falsely accused; sexual ethics in a committed relationship.
Informed autonomy, consent, care, tikkun olam in small ways (the council fixing an injustice).
Truthfulness, honoring the wronged, effort and humility.
frames.concerns: Haya and lowering the gaze: dating, kissing, sexual jokes and premarital relations (ch. 220) are core plot; the cosplay chapter (ch. 112).

frames.aligns: Satya (truth) wins; respect for elders where earned; a love story with a folktale frame.
frames.concerns: Love chosen against family arrangement (ch. 249) can be read differently by families who value arranged marriage; premarital relations; modesty.

frames.aligns: Pride and craving for "winning" cause suffering; right speech replaces manipulation; compassion for the outcast.
frames.concerns: Fourth precept: much comic false speech; third precept concerns vary on the unmarried couple.

frames.aligns: Sach (truthful living), service among friends, humility over ego (haumai).
frames.concerns: Sex only within marriage; premarital relations and sex jokes; ego and lust shown comically.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness "the foundation of all human virtues"; unity and friendship; no prejudice by class.
frames.concerns: Chastity before marriage; premarital relations framed positively; backbiting and rumor (shown as harmful).

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity) is the series' arc: masks of pride fall away. Built on the Kaguya-hime folktale; harmony in the group.
frames.concerns: No codified sexual ethic; shrine or kami content is minimal.

frames.aligns: Honor and keeping one's word; love between consenting partners; folklore frame.
frames.concerns: Early manipulation games; fortune-telling played for laughs.

frames.aligns: "Be faithful to your sexual partner," "Seek to live with the truth," "Honor and help your parents" (The Way to Happiness): the leads grow into truthful, faithful partners; Shirogane honors his father.
frames.concerns: Kaguya's break with her family; no psychiatry shown (recovery comes through friends), which aligns.

frames.aligns: Critique of misogyny, arranged marriage and class privilege; consent; mental-health struggles shown with care.
frames.concerns: Sexual jokes about high school characters; the minors' first night (ch. 220); comic spying and manipulation.

frames.aligns: Reason and wit; honesty as the foundation of relationships; justice for the falsely accused.
frames.concerns: Little pseudoscience; fortune-telling played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Hard work, merit over inherited wealth, honesty, loyalty, a stable couple who plan a future; respect for a loving father.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex and sex humor; a story siding with youth against family authority.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (Ishigami restored), free search for truth, justice, affirming relationships.
frames.concerns: Teasing manipulation outgrown; age-appropriateness of later volumes.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against arbitrary authority (the Shinomiya brothers, arranged marriage) admired; consenting partners; vengeance on the wrongdoer Ogino is achieved through exposure.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) not shown; Ogino's photo threat condemned by the story too.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The leads' pride ("whoever confesses first loses") is the comic flaw the story dismantles (ch. 137, 148). Ishigami answers an insult to Otomo with his fists and is punished; the story vindicates his motive but resolves it through the council's investigation and exposure, not revenge (ch. 88).

Order vs freedom.evidence: School rules and Miko's disciplinary committee are treated with affection, and fair process helps Ishigami graduate. But the climax celebrates Kaguya's freedom from family control and arranged marriage (ch. 249-261).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen friends outrank blood family: the council is Kaguya's real family, while her brothers treat her as a tool. Shirogane's warm family is the exception, not the rule.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A poor student and an heiress meet as equals; class is overcome. Senpai-kohai respect and the president's role remain, and Gan'an earns late sympathy.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Reason, strategy and personal choice guide life; religion is incidental. The folktale frame and family dynasty are honored as story, not as authority.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression and emotional honesty are the highest goods; Shirogane's thrift and hard work are admired, but the arc is about learning to show feelings and choose one's own life.

folkways.japan: The elite-academy setting, senpai-kohai etiquette, the student council's authority, Valentine's and White Day customs, Christmas Eve as a couples' holiday, zaibatsu family dynasties and the Kaguya-hime folktale are Japanese norms the story treats as setting. The heavy pressure on reputation (Ishigami's shunning) reflects Japanese school culture as the story portrays it.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism. Lens labels below are my own framing unless a source is named.

series.title: Tokyo Revengers
series.native: 東京卍リベンジャーズ

publishers.name: Seven Seas
publishers.notes: 16 Volumes 2-in-1 Omnibus Edition - Complete | 2 Vols 2-in-1 Brilliant Full Color Edition - Ongoing

entry.heading: Tokyo Revengers
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never abandon your friends and never give up on someone, however far gone; real strength is heart and loyalty, not fists, and violence and revenge only feed a cycle that kills the people you love.

content.framing: Shown with consequences, but styled as cool

frames.aligns: Evil (Kisaki's manipulation, the Moebius assault) is shown as evil and not made attractive in itself (Inter Mirifica 7); forgiveness over revenge; hope that no one is beyond redemption; marriage as the happy ending (ch. 278).
frames.concerns: Gang belonging and style can make sin attractive; Baji's self-stabbing framed as loyal (CCC 2280-2283); defiance of parents.

frames.aligns: Repentance and the hope of restoring even the worst (Kisaki, Mikey); love as perseverance.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant fighting, language and gang glamour a concern; the passions (anger, pride, vengeance) run the cast; no reference to God's grace.

frames.aligns: Clear consequences for sin: every violent path ends in death or prison; loyalty and repentance.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails for much of the content (language, violence, gang culture); suicide framed as noble. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing its end; grace-like persistence toward the lost (Takemichi never gives up on Mikey); redemption of enemies.
frames.concerns: The redemption has no source beyond human will and time travel; gang life is styled as cool.

frames.aligns: Clear moral stakes; deliverance-like rescue of a person consumed by darkness (Mikey).
frames.concerns: Holiness standards (language, worldliness, gang identity); "dark impulses" shown as an inherited force, not a spiritual battle; a religious symbol worn as a gang mark. Views range widely.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echo: good intentions keep producing worse futures; common grace allows valuing the story's insight on sin's spread.
frames.concerns: Self-stabbing framed as honorable (WLC Q136); the reset ending suggests humans can undo sin by their own effort.

frames.aligns: Law shown sharply: every attempt to fix things by works fails; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: The gospel answer is human persistence, not grace; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious about language and violence than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace has an echo in characters who change when someone refuses to give up on them; concern for neglected youth.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches would avoid the language and gang content; the "diversions" test of the General Rules. UMC families more open.

frames.aligns: Evil judged by framing: violence breeds loss; friendship and forgiveness win; marriage at the end.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes framed as honorable; gang glamour. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: The hero rarely wins by violence; he absorbs beatings and refuses to give up (ANN: he "saves the day (usually) without resorting to violence"); revenge is rejected (ch. 61).
frames.concerns: The world the story celebrates is organized around fighting; separation from worldly media makes this a likely avoid for Old Order families; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and repentance; friendship and marriage as the goal (ch. 278); protecting women.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: language, violence and gang culture may not invite the Spirit; suicide framed as loyalty. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Consequences of sin and the hope of restoration.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": constant fighting and gang identity; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; alcohol and tobacco shown.

frames.aligns: Love, loyalty and the rejection of revenge.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question whether entertainment features what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5); gang loyalty as identity; a religious symbol used for a gang.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts hatred; no one is beyond reform.
frames.concerns: Violence, fear and death are dwelt on as powerful forces; "stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Critique of how violence and neglect trap youth; empathy for orphans and outcasts (Izana, Kakucho; Tenjiku becomes a nonprofit for orphans, ch. 278).
frames.concerns: Women mainly as motivations or victims; the off-page sexual assault as a plot device; the manji edit debate.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah: every character can turn back; honoring parents (Hina's father is shown with sympathy); protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Nivul peh (coarse language) and violence; suicide framed as honorable; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether. The manji may also cause distress in homes that associate the shape with the Nazi swastika, though it is a different, Buddhist symbol.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah, loyalty, rejecting revenge, tikkun olam echoes in the reformed final timeline.
frames.concerns: Language and violence; suicide scenes; the manji's resemblance to the Nazi symbol may prompt questions.

frames.aligns: Hope that people and societies can be repaired; empathy for neglected youth.
frames.concerns: Women's limited role; the manji edits raise questions about context and education.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, protecting women, forgiveness preferred over revenge (Qur'an 42:40), repentance.
frames.concerns: Self-stabbing framed as loyal (Qur'an 4:29); alcohol and tobacco shown neutrally; foul language; the bathhouse scene (anime) under lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Karma: actions ripple across timelines; duty to friends; restoring order (dharma) after chaos.
frames.concerns: Gang violence is rajasic and tamasic in the Gita's terms (chapter 17); a sacred symbol (the swastika is also sacred in Hinduism) used as a gang emblem.

frames.aligns: Cycles of violence and their causes; Mikey's dark impulses as inherited karma; Baji ending a revenge cycle; compassion for enemies.
frames.concerns: A temple symbol, the manji, is worn as a gang emblem and was edited out abroad; killing and fighting throughout break the first precept.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude and loyalty; purification through renewal at the end.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity; little else.

frames.aligns: Standing up for the weak; anger (krodh) and ego (ahankar) shown as destructive in Mikey and Kisaki; seva-like care for orphans in the ending.
frames.concerns: Gang fighting for status rather than to defend the oppressed.

frames.aligns: Unity and reconciliation: rival gangs end up as friends and colleagues (ch. 278).
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence and to avoiding partisanship; gang rivalry runs the story.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "Do not murder," "Be worthy of trust," "Help take care of children" (Izana's orphans).
frames.concerns: The heroes are gang members whose way of life breaks the precept "Do not do anything illegal"; Mikey's dark impulses and suicidality are met by friendship rather than psychiatry, which some Scientologists may note favorably.

frames.aligns: Harm returns on the doer (threefold-law echoes in the time loop); loyalty and community.
frames.concerns: Harm none: the gang code harms many. No stereotyping of pagans.

frames.aligns: Critique of the violence cycle and of toxic masculinity softened by vulnerability (Butwhytho: "the value of vulnerability"); empathy for neglected kids.
frames.concerns: Few women; Hina and Emma mostly as motivation or victims; rape used as plot backstory; suicide imagery; Common Sense Media 15+.

frames.aligns: Human agency to change outcomes; friendship and reason over revenge; no supernatural judge.
frames.concerns: Time travel as a plot device rather than science; suicide scenes need mental-health framing; violence as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honor, protecting women, keeping promises, marriage and work at the end; Hina's father defended as right.
frames.concerns: Delinquency and defiance of school and police; gang life as a substitute for family; coarse language.

frames.aligns: Antiauthoritarian rebels and chosen loyalty; protection of the vulnerable (Satanic Temple Tenet 1); Church of Satan's "responsibility to the responsible."
frames.concerns: The story rejects revenge (Church of Satan teaching favors answering harm) and prizes self-sacrifice for the group over the self.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of the "worst" (Kisaki and Izana redeemed in ch. 278); justice for neglected youth.
frames.concerns: Violence as the medium; few women; manji context.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults and challenges are answered with fists; gang honor and "the path of a true delinquent" (Draken to Osanai, ch. 16) are celebrated. Baji's death to end a revenge cycle (ch. 61) and Takemichi's refusal to fight for pride pull it back from 10.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The heroes live outside school and law, ride motorcycles and fight freely; inside the gang, rank and a code bind them.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The gang is a sworn family; loyalty to one's own (founders, "brothers," sisters) outranks rules that apply to all. Pah-chin stabs Osanai for his friends (ch. 16); the Toman code protects its own.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Commanders, captains and division ranks; deference to Mikey as leader. Mikey's ideal of a gang where everyone matters softens it (from general knowledge; to verify).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Little religion; a delinquent tradition and code rather than faith; the ending is a secular, modern life.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Style, motorcycles and rebellion as self-expression, balanced by sacrifice, loyalty and toughness.

folkways.japan: The yankī and bōsōzoku subculture (embroidered tokkōfuku coats, motorcycle gangs, school delinquents), senpai-kohai hierarchy, and Shōwa-era nostalgia are Japanese genre conventions (Nippon.com traces the line from Be-Bop High School). The manji is a common Buddhist sign in Japan, used to mark temples on maps, and was also teen slang around 2016 (Kotaku). Readers outside Japan may see these as setting rather than message.

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (gang-as-family), Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (critiqued), Existentialism, Confucian ethics.

entry.heading: Dandadan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with kindness toward people, spirits and outsiders alike: stand by your friends, protect the vulnerable, eat well after hard work, and do not let fear or other people's mockery decide who you are.

content.framing: Condemned (assaults, framed as villainy); Neutral (gags and fan service)

frames.aligns: Predators and child sacrifice are clearly evil; kindness, loyalty and mercy to the suffering dead; the dignity of the bullied.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and the medium's practice shown as good and effective (CCC 2115-2117); sexual assault sometimes played for laughs, against Inter Mirifica 7's rule that evil not be made attractive or trivial.

frames.aligns: Struggle against cruelty and lust in the villains; compassion for the dead; repentance and reconciliation (Momo and Seiko).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit contact shown as heroic; evil spirits taken as real in the tradition, so yokai and "demons" played as allies or jokes are a concern. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the nudity and assault scenes a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Clear villains; standing up for the bullied; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Occult practice (Deuteronomy 18:10-12) shown as the heroine's family calling; crude sexual humor and frequent nudity of teens. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Kindness and respect as the core message (Reactor: "a story about boundaries and respect"); outsiders welcomed.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and spells, which many evangelicals separate from Tolkien-style magic; sexual menace used repeatedly (ANN).

frames.aligns: Courage, protection of friends, evil spirits defeated.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": demons, curses, spirit possession (Okarun by Turbo Granny), a medium and talismans, all shown as helpful when used by the heroes. Views range by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace: the story's moral sense (kindness, protecting the weak, justice for abusers) is real; human evil (Kito family, the blackmailing teacher) is shown plainly.
frames.concerns: Occult practice shown as good; WLC Q139 on "lascivious... books, pictures" applies to the fan service and nudity.

frames.aligns: Fantasy is often accepted; friends bearing one another's burdens; the vulnerable protected.
frames.concerns: Occult forbidden under the second commandment (Large Catechism), and here it is the heroine's training; sixth-commandment concerns with the content. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy toward the suffering, including ghosts; social holiness: the poor (Silky), the bullied, the exploited student.
frames.concerns: Occult practice endorsed; Wesley's General Rules on diversions that "cannot be used in the name of the Lord Jesus." Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing: predators, sacrifice cults and fake priests are condemned; imagination valued in the tradition (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: The occult is not just fantasy here: a medium's craft, exorcism and gods' borrowed power are the heroes' tools; sexual menace played as gags at times. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.

frames.aligns: Compassion for enemies and the dead; community of misfits caring for one another; humility.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool; occult practice; sexual content against plain modesty. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family love (Seiko and Momo; Silky and her daughter); kindness; service.
frames.concerns: Occult and spirit contact avoided by members; For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit, and the nudity and sexual gags conflict with chastity standards. Members vary.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized: bullied outsiders, a poor single mother, a student exploited by a teacher; abusers held to account.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence as a recurring plot device (The Mary Sue); occult rarely a focus.

The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so ghosts of the dead shown as real, grieving and "passing on" (ch. 17, 124-125), and a medium as a hero, run against teaching on the state of the dead and spiritualism.
Spiritism, magic and spirit possession are the series' core and are shown positively, a major concern in jw.org counsel (Galatians 5:19-21); violence and sexual content.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; kindness overcomes monsters; compassion for the grieving.
frames.concerns: Fear, curses and evil shown as real powers; spiritualism rejected as error in the tradition.

frames.aligns: Protection of the vulnerable; honoring a grandparent; condemnation of child sacrifice (echoing the Torah's rejection of Molech worship).
frames.concerns: A medium who deals with the dead is the heroine's teacher, and the heroine trains in the same craft (Deuteronomy 18:10-11 forbids the ov and yidoni); tzniut makes the nudity and sexual content a major concern. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Kindness, protection of the vulnerable, honoring a grandparent; abusers held to account.
frames.concerns: Sorcery forbidden but fantasy generally accepted; here the medium's practice is presented as real; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes: the friends repair harm and help the grieving; outsiders included; abusers exposed.
frames.concerns: Repeated sexual menace aimed at a teen girl; crude humor.

frames.aligns: Kindness, loyalty, standing up to oppressors; harm to children condemned; jinn-like spirits are familiar in Islamic belief.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) and spirit contact shown positively and used by the heroes; borrowed power of local gods; suicide in backstories (forbidden, Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Spirits and deities as part of the world; compassion for suffering beings; respect for an elder teacher (Seiko as a guru figure); black magic used for harm is condemned (curse-using groups, v25).
frames.concerns: Little message conflict beyond the sexual gags; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the crude content.

frames.aligns: Compassion for all beings, including ghosts and monsters; attachment as the root of the ghosts' suffering, released when they "pass on" (Silky, ch. 17); right effort rewarded.
frames.concerns: Violence is the usual solution; sexual misconduct (third precept) by villains is shown and sometimes made comic.

frames.aligns: Defending the vulnerable; the five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) shown in villains (Serpoians, Kito men, the teacher).
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic and superstition, and here they are the heroes' tools; lust is a constant source of jokes.

frames.aligns: Kindness, unity among very different people (humans, yokai, aliens), the equality of women and men (Momo as the strongest fighter early on).
frames.concerns: Spiritualism and occult discouraged; constant fighting; the call to a "chaste and holy life" weighs against the sexual humor.

frames.aligns: Kami, spirits and yokai are part of the world and treated with respect; gratitude to the god whose power Seiko borrows (temple visits); talismans on a torii gate; sincerity (makoto) in the leads; restless dead pacified.
frames.concerns: Fake priests and curse-users abuse the sacred, but the story condemns them; crude humor and nudity sit outside shrine decorum.

frames.aligns: Magic shown as a real, protective, ethical practice; a wise-woman grandmother as a hero; curses used to harm are condemned ("harm none"); folk spirits respected rather than demonized.
frames.concerns: Sexual threats and exploitation of teens, against the tradition's ethic of consent.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "Do not murder," protect the young, "Be worthy of trust"; the immortal spirit and many lives are familiar ideas.
frames.concerns: Violence as the usual solution; sexual content.

frames.aligns: Outsiders and the bullied included; a strong female lead; adult sexual predators and an exploitative teacher held to account; poverty and debt shown with empathy.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of teen characters and repeated sexual assault as plot driver (ANN; The Mary Sue); safe-messaging concerns with suicide backstories.

frames.aligns: Kindness, friendship, reason in tactics; the worth of a finite life; empathy for the marginalized.
frames.concerns: Spirit mediums and curses shown as real (fiction, but worth naming); exploitation in the sexual gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, protection of the weak, respect for a grandmother who raised the heroine; predators punished.
frames.concerns: Crude sexual humor and nudity aimed at a teen audience; authority figures often corrupt or absent; some religious conservatives object to the occult.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of everyone, including monsters and misfits; pluralism (humans, yokai and aliens cooperating); justice for the exploited.
frames.concerns: Sexual threat to a teen as recurring device; violence as solution.

frames.aligns: Irreverence toward authority and taboo; religion used to control (sacrifice cult, fake priest) exposed; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); self-chosen identity for outsiders.
frames.concerns: Harm to children is condemned in the Eleven Rules, and the story sometimes treats sexual threats to teens lightly; altruistic self-risk over self-interest.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Momo answers bullies directly (ch. 1) and the friends fight back, but revenge is not celebrated: the Evil Eye's vengeance is pitied and tamed (ch. 49-61), and Silky is released through compassion (ch. 17).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Teens act on their own judgment; institutions (school, police) barely help, and adult authorities are often the danger (Kito family; the gym teacher, v20-22).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Grandmother and granddaughter, a mother's love for her daughter, and a found family of friends come first; strangers and even monsters are also helped (Seiko: help others in trouble).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The friend group is flat and mixes social classes and species; Seiko is respected as an expert, not for rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Folk religious practice is real and passed from grandmother to granddaughter; but the story is modern, irreverent and full of science-fiction aliens, and harmful "tradition" (sacrifice) is condemned.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Okarun's and Kinta's obsessions and Momo's gyaru style are accepted; tolerance of the different (yokai, aliens) is the core message.

folkways.japan: Yokai, urban legends (Turbo Granny and Acrobatic Silky are based on real Japanese internet legends), Shinto and Buddhist practice, gyaru and otaku subcultures, and meal-as-reward scenes are Japanese context. A grandmother medium (a figure like the reiba or itako of Japanese folk religion; from general knowledge, to verify) is ordinary in that setting and not presented as exotic.

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk), Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics (kindness and courage), Expressive individualism (outsiders accepted as they are).

entry.heading: Hunter x Hunter
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a chosen adventure shared with friends. The story questions whether humans are better than the "monsters" they hunt, and it shows that strength, revenge and even goodness can become destructive when they turn obsessive.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the weak: a blind, poor girl changes a tyrant (Komugi). The Rose reads as a warning about weapons of mass destruction, in line with Church teaching against them (Pacem in Terris; Pope Francis at Nagasaki, 2019) (from general knowledge; to verify). Revenge shown as self-destroying.
frames.concerns: Netero's suicide to trigger the bomb (CCC 2280-2283); moral grayness can make evil attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); Hisoka's predatory fixation; gender questions (Alluka) read against Church teaching.

frames.aligns: The passions (wrath, pride) destroy Gon and the King until humility enters; repentance-like change in Meruem.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): constant body horror and cannibalism; Hisoka's lust for violence; a Bodhisattva image as power.

frames.aligns: Human sinfulness named ("bottomless malice within the human heart," ch. 298; compare Jeremiah 17:9); friendship and loyalty; consequences for revenge.
frames.concerns: Moral ambiguity without a clear good side; heroic violence as fun; Hisoka; gender-fluid characters; "false gods" (Family Friendly Gaming). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; strong picture of total human failure and of grace-like change through the weak (1 Corinthians 1:27).
frames.concerns: No source of grace beyond human kindness; moral grayness; violence and cannibalism; Hisoka.
Nen as spiritual life energy, a Bodhisattva figure, prayer used as a power source, an entity (Nanika) that grants wishes: some churches see these as "open doors." Views range widely.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: humanity's "bottomless malice" (ch. 298); no character is purely good. Common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Self-murder to win (WLC Q136); no redemption beyond the human; images of a Bodhisattva.

frames.aligns: Law shown without gospel: everyone is caught in cruelty; mercy comes from outside the strong (Komugi). Two kingdoms: the Hunter Association as a flawed worldly authority.
frames.concerns: Netero's suicide; violence as entertainment. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace has an echo in Meruem's growing conscience; works of mercy (Killua and Alluka healing Gon, ch. 333-335).
frames.concerns: Revenge and violence; Hisoka. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Fantasy that judges evil by framing; a just-war question at the heart of the arc (Article 37).
frames.concerns: Netero's suicide; weapons of mass destruction; Hisoka. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender (Alluka).

frames.aligns: The most transforming character is nonviolent (Komugi); the Rose shows violence corrupting even the "good" side; revenge ruins Gon.
frames.concerns: Violence as fun and as the main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency and choice; friendship; the King's change through love.
frames.concerns: Absent and abusive parents; suicide-bomb; violence; Hisoka's innuendo. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Critique of nuclear-style weapons and of human cruelty to the weak; sympathy for gender-diverse characters; dignity of a disabled girl.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; Hisoka's predatory framing; Plugged In's note on possible racial stereotypes.
"By beholding we become changed": cannibalism, gore and horror; Nen as spiritual power.

frames.aligns: Love, loyalty, peace over war in the end.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5); wish-granting entity and spirit-like powers (Galatians 5:19-21).
Fear, disease, poison and death are shown as real and dominant forces.

frames.aligns: Human capacity for evil named (yetzer hara); dignity of every life; critique of mass-destruction weapons.
frames.concerns: Suicide to kill an enemy; cannibalism and gore; Hisoka's innuendo; tzniut concerns; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Yetzer hara and teshuvah-like change (Meruem); kavod habriyot for the weak (Komugi).
Tikkun olam: protecting the vulnerable; critique of tyranny and WMD; dignity of gender-diverse characters.
Mercy, humility, respect for the weak; pride brought low.
frames.concerns: Netero's suicide to kill an enemy (Qur'an 4:29); a Bodhisattva figure; gender-fluid characters; Hisoka.

frames.aligns: Karma-like logic: vows have costs (Gon, Kurapika); Netero's devotion and gratitude; ahimsa-like turn in Meruem.
frames.concerns: Little message conflict; the gore may read as tamasic.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment destroy (Gon's revenge, Kurapika); a Bodhisattva form (from general knowledge); compassion transforms a killer (Meruem); impermanence.
frames.concerns: Killing as the plot's tool; a Bodhisattva image used as a weapon may trouble some.

frames.aligns: The five vices (anger, ego, attachment) shown destroying characters; humility wins; defending the weak.
Unity of humankind and the critique of weapons of mass destruction; love across difference.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence: fighting is the core of the series.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in Gon and Komugi; gratitude in Netero's training.
frames.concerns: Death and blood as impurity; no shrine disrespect reported.

frames.aligns: Life energy as a power everyone has (Nen); nature and animals (Kite's bond with animals; Gon's island life); "harm none" echoed in the critique of the Rose.
The Way to Happiness: do not murder, safeguard and improve your environment; personal ability over limits.
frames.concerns: Killing everywhere; Gon's self-destruction. No psychiatry content found.

frames.aligns: Anti-war and anti-WMD reading (SlashFilm); sympathy for gender-diverse characters (Bakker thesis); critique of dictatorship and abusive families; disabled girl as genius.
frames.concerns: Hisoka's sexualized interest in children; Plugged In's note on two characters "stylized on racist stereotypes"; violence for younger teens.

frames.aligns: Meaning chosen in life itself (Togashi: characters who "found the meaning of life in the process rather than the result"); empathy across species; human cruelty faced honestly.
frames.concerns: Suicide and self-destruction need safe-messaging talk.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, gratitude, mentorship (Wing, Biscuit, Netero); friendship.
frames.concerns: Absent and abusive fathers, weak and corrupt institutions, moral relativism, gender-fluid characters, no clear good side.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of the enemy; free search for truth; sympathy for gender-diverse characters.
Self-determination (Ging, Killua leaving his family); skepticism of authority; meaning chosen by the self; compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) is pervasive, though condemned; Netero sacrifices himself for the group.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge for honor or kin drives Kurapika and Gon, and both pay heavily for it (ch. 75-80 likely; ch. 305-309). Hisoka's duels are personal. The story neither celebrates nor dismisses honor; it counts the cost.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Hunters roam freely with a license that opens doors; Gon, Killua and Ging choose their own paths; controlling orders (ant castes, dictatorship, Zoldyck house rules) are critiqued.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen friendship outranks blood (Killua leaves his family); loyalty to kin still matters (Killua protecting Alluka, ch. 319-339). The Hunter Association as a civic body is flawed.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A blind commoner humbles the king (ch. 243-258); the ant hierarchy collapses; the Association's chairman is chosen by election (ch. 319-339 likely). Mentors are respected.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A secular world: Nen is a learnable system with rules; religion is personal (Netero's prayers, ch. 265) and in the background.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A deadly, food-chain world, but the heroes pursue chosen adventures and meaning "in the process rather than the result" (Togashi).

folkways.japan: Mentor-student respect (Wing, Biscuit, Netero), gungi and shogi-style board culture, the shonen tournament structure, and Buddhist imagery around Netero reflect Japanese norms. The story's suspicion of family duty and institutions is more its own message than a Japanese default.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Might makes right (critiqued), Expressive individualism, Utilitarianism (explored).
