entry.heading: 20th Century Boys (with 21st Century Boys)
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Evil is shown but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); a false messiah exposed; the Pope and a church shown as good; repentance and atonement for many characters.
frames.concerns: A staged resurrection and divine claims can read as a parody of Christ's, judged by framing; the secular reading that every messiah is suspect.

frames.aligns: Deception, pride and self-deification condemned; repentance at the end of life (Yamane, Sadakiyo).
frames.concerns: Mockery of holy things is serious in the tradition: a fake resurrection and god-worship need framing. Guarding the senses for the dread and deaths.

frames.aligns: Clear warning against false prophets; ordinary believers resisting a captured state; honesty and confession.
frames.concerns: Secular tone; psychic powers; drinking and a mafia setting. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A cautionary tale about cults and manufactured crises; confession and reconciliation in Kenji's apology.
frames.concerns: The story's salvation is human and scientific (Bancha's "secular savior"); its heroes are also "desacralized messiahs."

frames.aligns: Spiritual deception exposed; false signs and wonders condemned.
frames.concerns: Psychic powers (Kanna, spoon bending, a "God" psychic) shown as real at least in part; no spiritual battle beyond the human one. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in how easily crowds follow; idolatry of a man exposed; common grace in good art.
frames.concerns: Secular framing of salvation by science; self-destructive acts (Maruo's near bombing).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: a cult that seizes the state's sword is shown as monstrous; law and gospel echoed in confession and forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Little; LCMS and WELS families may want more care with the occult elements.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: ordinary people standing against injustice; works of mercy (Kiriko treating victims).
frames.concerns: Drinking, gambling and a mafia setting; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: deception and tyranny condemned; a strong literary mystery.
frames.concerns: A parody resurrection and pope plot, read in context.

frames.aligns: The climax turns on confession and refusing to harm innocents, not on killing; a critique of state religion and mass conformity.
frames.concerns: Guns, bombs and a mafia alliance as heroes' tools; conservative groups avoid popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency and honesty; warnings against secret combinations (Ether 8) map onto the cult-party; family love (Kenji and Kanna).
Critique of propaganda, scapegoating and captured institutions; care for the sick (Kiriko); diverse cast.
frames.concerns: Few women in power until Kanna; little on structural causes.

frames.aligns: End-time deception and a false world ruler echo the tradition's prophecy themes; the virtual world is shown as illusion.
frames.concerns: Prophecy treated as a human fabrication; psychic powers; fear-heavy content. "By beholding we become changed."

frames.aligns: Exposes false religion allied with politics, a theme the tradition stresses; nationalism and party loyalty shown as dangerous.
frames.concerns: Violence and psychic powers; the heroes' armed resistance against neutrality.

frames.aligns: Truth exposing error is the plot's engine; fear shown as the cult's weapon.
frames.concerns: Disease, contagion and death are central and real; a vaccine is the savior.

frames.aligns: Idolatry of a man condemned; lies and slander (lashon hara) as the cult's tools; repentance (teshuvah) open.
frames.concerns: Bar, mafia and red-light settings; time spent on secular entertainment. Haredi homes may restrict it.

frames.aligns: False prophets exposed; memory and responsibility across generations.
Critique of authoritarian movements and scapegoating; tikkun olam in ordinary people's resistance.
A man claiming divinity and being worshipped is condemned, in line with tawhid; deception exposed; forgiveness and repentance.
frames.concerns: Alcohol, gambling and a drug offer; psychic powers; red-light settings.

frames.aligns: Adharma of a deceiving ruler exposed; duty of ordinary people; karma-like consequences of a childhood wrong.
Craving for attention and ego drive the villain; delusion of the crowd; right speech and honesty. Aum used Buddhist and Hindu language (general knowledge), so some families will note the parallel.
frames.concerns: Violence and killing by heroes and villains; the story does not offer a Buddhist path.

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) and deception condemned; standing up for the oppressed.
Independent investigation of truth against blind following; unity of humanity against division; low glorification of violence.
Sincerity (makoto) in Kenji; respect for community and childhood bonds.
frames.concerns: Little Shinto content; death and blood as impurity.

frames.aligns: No witches or pagans stereotyped; "harm none" against mass killing; personal responsibility.
The Way to Happiness precepts: do not murder, be worthy of trust, seek to live with the truth; a drug offer is rejected.
frames.concerns: A new religious movement is shown as a sinister cult with re-education and "banishment"; the church's own sources object to "cult" labels for new religions (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Warning about authoritarian populism, propaganda, conspiracy thinking and scapegoating the unvaccinated; diverse cast; a young woman leads.
frames.concerns: Few women among the old gang; little on structural injustice.

frames.aligns: Bancha (2020): the series "promotes secularist values"; science as savior; miracles debunked; critical thinking about every messiah.
Loyalty, courage, keeping promises, nostalgia for an ordinary childhood; a warning against mass movements and a captured state.
frames.concerns: Skepticism toward all religion; outlaw heroes.

frames.aligns: Free and responsible search for truth against dogma; inherent worth of the scapegoated.
Skepticism of supernatural claims and religious authority; rebellion against arbitrary power; rock music as self-assertion; protection of children.
frames.concerns: The heroes act for others more than for the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Kenji answers the villain with an apology, not revenge (21st Century Boys); Maruo stops short of a suicide bombing. A childhood slight that festered into hatred is the villain's origin (TV Tropes, toy badge).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The regime's total order is the evil; rock music, outlaws and a citizen resistance are celebrated (Wikipedia; EBSCO).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen kin (the childhood gang) and family (Kenji and Kanna) drive the heroes, but the stakes are all of humanity.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A flat circle of friends against a leader-worship hierarchy; deference to Friend is the cult's sin.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Miracles debunked, science saves (Bancha 2020); nostalgia is warm but distrusted.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A survival plot, but music, memory and personal conscience are the values the story lifts up.

folkways.japan: Showa-era nostalgia, Expo '70, school-group friendships and Japan's post-1995 anxiety about new religious movements after the Aum sarin attack are Japanese contexts the story draws on; readers elsewhere may see the cult mainly as a general warning about charismatic movements.

entry.heading: Monster
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Dignity of every life (CCC 2258) in Tenma's choice and in saving Johan; evil depicted but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); conversion of Eva and Lunge. Catholic writer Matthew Tan reads it as a story about communion versus isolation (Humanum Review).
frames.concerns: Many suicides and suicide games; Tenma's resolve to kill; dread with no explicit grace.

frames.aligns: Repentance shown in many lives; Tenma's humility and self-giving; evil as personal and deceiving.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against long dread, murder and despair; Antichrist imagery handled as a thriller motif.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a hero who will not take vengeance (Romans 12:19); the worth of the outcast (a Turkish worker, orphans).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 for the murders, drinking and suicide content; T+ and TV-MA ratings. Views vary by family.

frames.aligns: Gaheret (Beneath the Tangles): evil is real but limited, "The One who saves is immensely greater than the one who kills."
frames.concerns: Salvation in the story is human and medical, not explicitly Christ; the open ending.

frames.aligns: Real, personal evil that tempts and deceives; deliverance from despair (Nina).
frames.concerns: The Antichrist motif with no spiritual battle; occult-sounding "nameless monster" picture books used for mind control; a dark open ending. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Total depravity in how easily people are drawn to Johan; common grace in Tenma's mercy and in skilled art; providence-like irony in the ending.
frames.concerns: Lascivious content is minor; long violence and despair.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Tenma's guilt and the grace of being forgiven by those he wronged; vocation as a physician.
frames.concerns: Little beyond the dread; LCMS and WELS families may weigh the suicide content more.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and social holiness (Doctors Without Borders at the end; care for immigrants and orphans).
frames.concerns: Drinking, gun violence; holiness churches more cautious under the General Rules.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: a serious literary thriller that condemns cruelty and honors mercy.
Tenma never kills; the climax is healing an enemy; a critique of state violence (Kinderheim) and nationalism (neo-Nazis).
frames.concerns: Tenma carries a gun and intends to kill; heavy violence; conservative groups avoid popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency and choice over upbringing (EBSCO); worth of souls (D&C 18:10); family and identity restored (Nina's graduation).
frames.concerns: Alcohol, suicide themes, nudity in photos (anime). Does it invite the Spirit (For the Strength of Youth)?

frames.aligns: Equal worth across class and nationality (the Turkish worker, orphans); critique of xenophobia, neo-Nazis and abusive institutions.
frames.concerns: Few women in power; little on structural repair.

frames.aligns: The sanctity of life and a healer as hero fit the health-ministry tradition; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": long murder, alcohol and despair content; Antichrist motif used as suspense.

frames.aligns: Exposes nationalism, political power and violence as destructive; values life.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) is constant; spiritism-like mind control in the picture books; blood and surgery are central (members accept surgery without transfusion; not raised by the story).

frames.aligns: Love overcoming hatred; truth exposing error.
frames.concerns: Surgery and medicine save lives at the core of the story; fear, disease, injury and death fill it; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh: saving a life overrides almost everything; "whoever saves one life saves a world" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5); teshuvah for Eva and Lunge; neo-Nazis condemned.
frames.concerns: Time on secular entertainment; immodest images; Haredi homes may restrict it. Holocaust-era themes (a new Hitler) need care.

frames.aligns: Sanctity of life; memory and names as moral duty; neo-Nazis and genocidal plans condemned.
frames.concerns: Little; no antisemitic tropes reported (to verify).

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in Doctors Without Borders; anti-racism; equal dignity.
"Whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32); a Turkish Muslim community shown as victims of hate, not as villains; mercy and justice.
frames.concerns: Alcohol throughout; immodest images (anime); suicide content.

frames.aligns: Ahimsa and dharma of the healer; karma-like consequences of a choice; the self beyond a name.
Compassion without exception; craving and ignorance as roots of harm; Johan's "nameless" emptiness read against non-self.
frames.concerns: Killing on many pages; Johan's nihilism could be confused with emptiness (sunyata), which it is not.

frames.aligns: Sarbat da bhala (welfare of all); seva in Tenma's service; ego (haumai) in the hospital director.
Oneness of humanity against racism and nationalism; service as worship; low glorification of violence.
Sincerity (makoto) in Tenma; gratitude and purity of heart.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity throughout; no Shinto content.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" against manipulation and killing; no witches stereotyped.

The Way to Happiness precepts: safeguard and improve your health, do not murder, be worthy of trust; drugging and mind-reshaping of children at Kinderheim 511 shown as monstrous, in line with the church's critique of psychiatric abuse (CCHR).
frames.concerns: A psychotherapist (Reichwein) and a criminal psychologist (Gillen) are sympathetic heroes, and therapy helps characters heal, which the church's opposition to psychiatry rejects (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Anti-racism, critique of authoritarian states and neo-Nazis, care for refugees and orphans; equal medical care regardless of status.
frames.concerns: Women mostly in supporting roles (Nina, Eva are strong); some reviewers find the ending unsatisfying.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person without appeal to the supernatural; science and medicine as service; eugenics and mind control condemned; choice over upbringing (EBSCO).
Anti-communist and anti-Nazi; duty, honor and perseverance; family and the right to one's name; law officers who serve truth (Lunge).
frames.concerns: An outlaw hero for most of the story; little faith content.

frames.aligns: The first principle, "inherent worth and dignity of every person," is the hero's motto; justice and compassion; free search for meaning.

The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and on acting by reason; the Church of Satan's Eleven Rules forbid harming children, and Kinderheim is condemned; skepticism of state and ideological authority.
frames.concerns: Tenma's mercy to a man who harms others conflicts with the Satanic Bible's "responsibility to the responsible" and rejection of turning the other cheek (from general knowledge; to verify).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: "All lives are equal" (Tenma's motto); Tenma gives up revenge and heals Johan (ch. 160-161, likely); justice goes to the police and courts (Lunge, ending).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Abusive state order (Kinderheim, secret police) is the evil, but lawful institutions are redeemed; Tenma's outlaw freedom is a burden, not an ideal.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Equal care for strangers, a migrant worker and the enemy; the ending is Doctors Without Borders. Twin bonds matter, but kin loyalty never overrides the duty to all.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The hospital hierarchy that ranks a mayor above a boy is the first wrong (ch. 1-3).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Medicine, detection and psychology solve the case; religion is mostly motif.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Tolerance, memory, names and quality of life ("A Happy Table," ch. 131) are lifted up against a survival-and-fear world.

folkways.japan: The story is set almost entirely in Germany and the Czech Republic and draws on European post-Cold-War history rather than Japanese norms. Tenma's quiet self-sacrifice and his family's expectation that he inherit a hospital (Monster wiki) reflect Japanese duty and family hierarchy as context; the series' message points away from status and rank.

entry.heading: [Oshi no Ko]
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Mixed and debated. The story shows that lies told for love can become true, that fame and online crowds devour young people, and that revenge consumes the one who pursues it. Its ending honors Aqua's self-sacrifice for his sister and has Ruby carry her mother's "lie" of love forward on stage.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; the ending is debated
Critiqued in the story; heavy franchise outside it

frames.aligns: Exposes exploitation and degradation of persons (Ethics in Communications); dignity of the harassed; Ai's love for her children; forgiveness in her last message.
frames.concerns: Aqua's murder-suicide presented as peaceful self-giving (CCC 2280-2283, 2302 on anger and revenge); reincarnation as premise; teen pregnancy without comment on marriage; sibling romance (ch. 123, 143).

frames.aligns: Lies and passions (vainglory, anger) shown to destroy; mercy in Ai's last words.
frames.concerns: Revenge never repented of; self-destruction framed as rest; rebirth instead of resurrection; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the deaths and the twin kisses a concern.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences: revenge costs Aqua his life; cruelty online is shown as deadly.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation (Hebrews 9:27); suicide framed as heroic; sibling romance; profanity. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Ai's lie as an imperfect faith met with grace (John 4; Matthew 5:43-48). Honest look at a fallen industry.
frames.concerns: No source of grace beyond human love; revenge and murder-suicide as climax; reincarnation; Ruby and Aqua (ch. 143).

frames.aligns: Clear exposure of exploitation and cruelty.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation and a possibly spirit-like child at Takachiho shown as real (to verify); suicide framed as sacrifice; "idol" devotion as the story's culture.

frames.aligns: Depravity throughout the industry and in every main character's motives; common grace in the art.
frames.concerns: Self-murder (WLC Q136) framed as noble; reincarnation; WLC Q139 on "lascivious" material for the romance scenes.

frames.aligns: Law exposed: everyone lies, everyone is exposed. Vocation of parents (Miyako) shown faithfully.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; revenge and self-destruction as resolution. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: protecting young workers from exploitation; care for the harassed.
frames.concerns: Revenge plot; murder-suicide; reincarnation; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Works judged by framing; strong critique of exploitation; Ai's love as a real good.
frames.concerns: Murder-suicide framed as resolution; reincarnation; the twin romance. Episcopal and ACNA families may weigh these differently.

frames.aligns: Critique of fame and worldliness; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Revenge is the main plot and ends in killing; separation from "the world" makes the entertainment setting itself a concern. Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Families matter; a mother's love lasts beyond death; exploitation of youth condemned.
frames.concerns: Teen pregnancy outside marriage without comment; reincarnation versus the plan of salvation; suicide; sibling romance; profanity.

frames.aligns: Structural sin: an industry that harms children, online mobs, unprotected labor; sympathy for a teen mother.
frames.concerns: Revenge and murder-suicide as resolution; the twin romance; Anime Feminist's point that the harassment arc omits misogyny and racism.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a corrupting industry; family love.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; suicide; revenge; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment.

frames.aligns: Exposes the world's corruption; love of family.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation and spirit-like elements; violence and self-destruction; the twin romance; profanity.
Fear, violence, death and harassment are dwelt on as powerful realities, against the teaching that they are not of God.

frames.aligns: Exposure of lashon hara as deadly (vol. 3 harassment arc); protecting life; honoring a mother.
frames.concerns: Suicide framed as sacrifice; revenge outside courts; tzniut (stage, kisses, sibling romance); many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Lashon hara condemned in effect; protecting the vulnerable; care for a mother's memory.
frames.concerns: Revenge and murder-suicide; the twin romance.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: exposing exploitation of youth and online cruelty; sympathy for a young mother.
frames.concerns: Revenge and murder-suicide as resolution; the twin romance.

frames.aligns: Backbiting and slander shown as deadly (Qur'an 49:12); protecting family; exposing exploitation.
frames.concerns: Suicide (Qur'an 4:29) and revenge outside justice; reincarnation versus resurrection; idol performance, music and romance; unmarried pregnancy without comment.

frames.aligns: Rebirth and unfinished karma drive the plot; a mother's devotion; the costs of attachment and revenge.
frames.concerns: Revenge and self-destruction as resolution; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the darkness.

frames.aligns: Rebirth; craving for fame (tanha) as suffering; anger and revenge as poisons that consume Aqua; Ai's compassion for her enemy.
frames.concerns: Killing as the plot's resolution (first precept); right speech violated throughout; entertainment avoided on precept days.

frames.aligns: The five vices shown destroying people: ego (fame), lust, anger (revenge), attachment, greed in the industry.
frames.concerns: Revenge and self-destruction as resolution; romance plot.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness as a theme; unity of a found family; exposure of backbiting.
frames.concerns: Revenge and violence; romance and the twin plot against a "chaste and holy life"; suicide.

frames.aligns: Takachiho, sacred landscape and a possibly divine child treated with respect (to verify); sincerity (makoto) versus the industry's falseness.
frames.concerns: Death and blood as impurity; revenge.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" in the critique of exploitation and harassment; rebirth as part of the cycle.
The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, do not murder, be trustworthy; exploitation and harassment condemned. Past lives are part of Scientology belief, so rebirth with memory is familiar.
frames.concerns: Murder-suicide as resolution; lies as a main tool; how the story frames mental-health care (to verify; the Church opposes psychiatry).

frames.aligns: Critique of exploitation of young women and child performers, reality-TV cruelty, stalker fandom, no-union labor; sympathy for a teen mother.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist: the harassment arc evokes Hana Kimura but leaves out misogyny and racism, and resolves it with a male rescuer; Kyoko Kimura's objection; the twin romance; the minor's abuse as villain backstory; violent ending.

frames.aligns: Free inquiry into how media manipulates; empathy for victims; reincarnation read as a fiction device.
frames.concerns: Murder-suicide framed as noble; revenge over courts and evidence.

frames.aligns: Critique of shallow celebrity culture and online mobs; a mother's love; protection of children.
frames.concerns: Teen pregnancy outside marriage normalized; absent fathers; revenge as private justice; the twin romance.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the harassed and exploited; justice for young workers.
frames.concerns: Violence and murder-suicide as resolution; the twin romance.

frames.aligns: Exposes abuse of children and the vulnerable (Eleven Rules; Satanic Temple Tenets on compassion and justice); distrust of power; self-determination.
frames.concerns: Aqua's self-destruction rather than self-preservation; harm done in pursuit of justice.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Aqua's lifelong revenge for his mother reads as honor-driven, yet the story shows it consuming him and has Ai's last message wish her betrayer self-love; harassment is answered by revealing the truth, not retaliation (vol. 3).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Industry rules (no dating, agency control) are shown as oppressive; performers seeking freedom to be themselves are sympathetic.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Mother, twins and adoptive parents come first; Aqua's final act puts his sister above law and life (ch. 162-164).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The hierarchy of producers, stars and agencies is shown abusing the young; Akasaka: "you can't go against the office manager."

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A modern, media-saturated setting; religion appears only as unexplained rebirth and a shrine; no tradition guides the characters.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Dreams of performing and authentic self-expression are celebrated (Ruby, Kana), though the cost of fame is shown.

folkways.japan: The idol "no-dating" rule, the agency system, senpai-kohai deference on set, tabloid culture and Japan's reality-TV and online harassment debates (after Terrace House) are Japanese industry norms the story criticizes from within; readers elsewhere will meet them as setting rather than as a message aimed at their own culture.

entry.heading: Dragon Ball (manga, 1984-1995)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one of joyful striving: train hard, keep getting stronger, enjoy the fight, protect your friends, forgive rivals and give former enemies a place at the table.

content.frequency: Constant in the second half; frequent in the first
content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as virtue), with deaths shown with consequences
Played for laughs; Roshi's lechery is mocked but rarely punished

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others (Vegeta, ch. 467; Piccolo shielding Gohan); mercy to defeated enemies; conversion of villains; tyrants condemned.
frames.concerns: Lechery and child-nudity gags played as harmless (ch. 2, 4), which Inter Mirifica 7 would see as making wrong attractive; resurrection by wish rather than grace; gods as fighters.

frames.aligns: Repentance and transformation of enemies (Piccolo, Vegeta); self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Fighting enjoyed for its own sake (the tradition treats killing as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); a "Demon King," a wizard (Babidi) and gods who can be out-powered treat the spiritual lightly; lust gags feed the "passions." Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on both halves.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance, loyalty, redemption arcs; tyrants defeated.
frames.concerns: Other gods shown as real (John 14:6); harassment gags go unpunished; drinking played for laughs, where many are teetotal. Many families would treat vols. 1-16 as off-limits for children.

frames.concerns: Beneath the Tangles: the series reinforces Japanese spiritual ideas; "Animism, reincarnation, and the such are part of life" in its world; answers "both yes and no." Movieguide (on the 2014 Battle of Gods film, not the manga) calls the worldview "very strong polytheistic pagan."

Many gods, a Demon King, wizards, magic orbs and an afterlife without one God, presented as the real order of the world; media as an "open door" makes this weigh heavily. Plugged In warns of "dark and disturbing spiritual fascinations."

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goodness (loyalty, sacrifice, mercy) in a non-Christian story.

frames.aligns: Redemption of former enemies; worth of every being; respect for many traditions.
frames.concerns: Harassment as comedy; Mr. Popo's design; mockery of a gay-coded villain. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Martial pride and the tournament code of honor run through the series; Vegeta's bloodline pride drives his arc. The story also honors mercy (sparing Frieza) and Vegeta's turn from pride to self-sacrifice (ch. 467).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Goku fights for the joy of it and does not seek command; each arc's hero is stronger but chooses not to rule (Philosophy essay). Gods are bureaucrats and mentors, not lawgivers, and Goku leaves home to train Uub (ch. 517-519).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Goku protects Earth because his friends live there. Former enemies join the circle (Piccolo, Vegeta, Buu). Family is present but often secondary to friends and training.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Tyrants who want to own others are destroyed (Frieza, Cell, Kid Buu). Rank exists among fighters and gods (Kais, Supreme Kai), but strength is earned by training, and rivals are welcomed as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A Buddhist, Taoist and folk cosmology (King Yama, Kami, halos) is setting, not worship; Toriyama said he did not think deeply about it. Capsule Corp technology and whatever works solve problems (Pragmatic lens).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Joyful striving is the life message: train, enjoy the fight, food and friends. Death is often reversible through the Dragon Balls, so security fears weigh lightly.

folkways.japan: The Jump formula of friendship, effort and victory, the master-and-disciple training model (Roshi, Kami) and the folk cosmology borrowed from Chinese and Japanese Buddhism reflect Japanese boys' manga norms of the 1980s and 1990s rather than the story's own argument.

entry.title: Innocent
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: A historical drama loosely based on the real Sanson family, hereditary executioners of Paris before the French Revolution. Gentle Charles-Henri Sanson recoils from the killing his inherited office demands but accepts it to protect his family, vowing to be the last executioner. His younger sister Marie-Joseph rebels against the gender rules of her time and seeks a place in the executions and at court.
entry.life_message: It holds up refusing to let birth, office or society dictate who you are, even at great personal cost.

content.note: Graphic executions with heavy blood, a father torturing his son by breaking his legs, and animal cruelty (ANN reviews; Manga Critic; AniList Gore 81%, Torture 79%).
Unrelenting, lingering depictions of suffering and death; critics call it harsh and not for the faint of heart (ANN; Manga Critic; AniList Tragedy 85%).
Several sex scenes, a group-sex panel, implied rape and incest, frequent nudity (ANN publisher content warning and Silverman review; MangaUpdates Rape, Nudity; AniList Nudity 71%).
Dark Horse edition rated 18+ partly for language (Manga Critic); frequency not detailed (to verify).

entry.title: Welcome to the N.H.K.
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Tatsuhiro Sato, a 22-year-old university dropout, has been a hikikomori (shut-in) for years and blames a conspiracy he calls the N.H.K. A mysterious girl, Misaki, offers to 'cure' him through nightly counseling sessions, while his otaku neighbor Yamazaki drags him into writing an erotic video game. Drugs, a pyramid scheme, an online suicide pact and his own paranoia pull him down before a fragile bond with Misaki gives both a reason to go on.
entry.life_message: It holds up the halting, unheroic step of staying alive and reaching out to one other person.

entry.title: Nijigahara Holograph
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Fifth-grader Arie Kimura tells classmates a fairy tale about a girl sent by God who is sacrificed to a monster in the Nijigahara tunnel; the bullied Arie is then pushed down a well by seven classmates and left in a coma. Told out of order across two timelines, the single volume follows those children as damaged adults, amid swarms of butterflies, hidden abuse and spiralling violence.

entry.premise: Childhood friends Yohei, Yui and Kei reunite in high school, but Kei returns with long hair and a girls' uniform, saying they are no longer a boy without claiming to be a girl. entry.title: Doubt
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Players of the phone game Rabbit Doubt meet offline and wake trapped in an abandoned psychiatric hospital, barcodes on their bodies and one of their group hanged. They must play a real version of the game and expose the 'wolf' among them as killings mount and secrets surface. The final twist reveals that the seemingly first victim, Rei, manipulated another girl through hypnosis to carry out revenge.
entry.life_message: It suggests that trust is fragile and hidden guilt eventually surfaces; survival depends on seeing through lies.

entry.premise: After a human hero slays the Demon Lord, the demon realm holds a tournament for a successor, and a human named Helck, who claims to hate humanity, enters. entry.title: Are You a Landmine, Chihara-san?
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: High school junior Kuroki ends up seated beside Mai Chihara, a girl in gothic 'landmine' (jirai-kei) fashion whom classmates assume is unstable and clingy. After she notices him, he discovers she is sweet, odd and earnest rather than dangerous. The episodic romantic comedy follows him getting to know her behind the reputation.

entry.title: Welcome to Ethics Class
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Mr. Takayanagi, a calm and enigmatic high school ethics teacher, meets students in crisis one by one and uses ethical thinking and philosophy to help them face their problems. The episodic seinen drama takes on serious issues that database tags list as bullying, suicide, sexual assault, drugs and delinquency. It was adapted into an NHK television drama in 2021.

entry.title: Brutal
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Hiroki Dan is a polite, well-liked homicide detective and the son of a former police chief. In secret he is a serial killer who tortures and kills people he believes the law cannot reach, such as abusers, rapists and a man profiting from his past murders. Each chapter is largely a self-contained case.
entry.life_message: It presents private, violent retribution against unpunished abusers as a dark fantasy of justice, without resolving whether it is justice.

entry.title: Trigun
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: On the desert planet Gunsmoke, the gunman Vash the Stampede carries a sixty-billion-double-dollar bounty for destroying the city of July, which he cannot clearly remember. Despite inhuman skill with a gun, he refuses to kill and uses his weapons to save lives, shadowed by two insurance agents and sometimes joined by the gun-toting priest Nicholas D. Wolfwood. This first three-volume series begins revealing his past and his twin brother Knives, continued in Trigun Maximum.

entry.premise: After two killings in a small town, high schooler Mizuki Aikawa confesses to murdering her best friend Mako. Her public defender, Yutaka Tsuji, finds contradictions, and the story moves back and forth in time to reveal sexual exploitation by Mako's uncle, an overbearing mother and a cover-up. entry.title: Campfire Cooking in Another World with My Absurd Skill
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Salaryman Tsuyoshi Mukouda is accidentally pulled into a fantasy kingdom alongside three summoned teenage 'Heroes'. Suspecting the kingdom wants to use them in its war, he slips away with a seemingly useless skill, an 'Online Supermarket' that delivers modern Japanese groceries. His cooking wins over a legendary wolf, Fel, then more familiars and even a group of goddesses, and the story follows their food-centered travels.

entry.premise: Teen martial artist Ranma Saotome fell into a cursed spring in China and now turns into a girl when splashed with cold water; his father becomes a panda. Their fathers' old pact engages Ranma to Akane Tendo so the two can inherit the family dojo, though neither wants it. entry.title: Ichi the Killer
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In Tokyo's Kabukicho, a manipulator called the Old Geezer uses Ichi, an emotionally broken young man conditioned to kill when he cries, to destroy the Anjo yakuza family. The family's enforcer Kakihara, a sadomasochist who lives for pain, hunts Ichi, and the two close in on each other through a chain of killings and torture. The seinen series inspired Takashi Miike's 2001 film and is known for ero guro content.

entry.heading: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Identity is a choice made under pressure: a person who belongs to two worlds can try to protect both, but the story counts the cost of that choice in pain and loss, and offers only a fragile hope that the two sides might one day live together.

content.framing: Neutral; predatory desire shown as menacing

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person, even the "monster"; critique of dehumanizing the outsider; evil (torture, revenge) shown as evil with consequences.
frames.concerns: Despair rather than hope dominates the original ending; revenge is pursued by several sympathetic characters; gratuitous gore in media is criticized by the Church ("Ethics in Communications").

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (hunger as a picture of a consuming passion); compassion for the enemy.
frames.concerns: Darkness without theosis or grace; strong concern about images that feed the passions; the church setting used for a cannibal scene (vol. 4-5) touches reverence for holy places.

frames.aligns: Clear depiction of sin's consequences; friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: No saving answer, only human striving; graphic violence and strong language (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles writers read Kaneki's arc as a search for redemption: "to be human means to feel pain." Evil framed as evil; mercy toward outsiders.
frames.concerns: The redemption remains unfinished; occasional nihilistic voices; gore and language.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between destructive and protective power.
frames.concerns: Ghouls are not demons, but the predatory, possession-like imagery (Rize "inside" Kaneki's mind, ch. 62-63, likely) can concern families attentive to spiritual warfare.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed: every faction, human and ghoul, is capable of atrocity; common grace lets families value a serious work by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: No providence or grace in view; vengeance taken into human hands (WLC on the sixth commandment).

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows people unable to save themselves. Two kingdoms: questions about the state's use of force.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer offered; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the outcast and the hunted; works of mercy (Anteiku feeding ghouls without killing).
frames.concerns: No grace named, and the hope of coexistence is left unfinished. Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus" makes the graphic content a heavy depiction concern for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan), less for many UMC families.

frames.aligns: Respect for the outsider; just-war questions (Article 37) about the CCG's campaign.
frames.concerns: Despair at the end; revenge cycles. Episcopal and ACNA families differ more on gender than on this content.

frames.aligns: The cycle of violence is shown as destroying everyone; Anteiku's nonviolent ethic and Kaneki's mother's "better to be hurt" echo nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Kaneki abandons that ethic and the story makes his violence effective. Conservative groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and the struggle of a divided nature; family love; service.
frames.concerns: A bleak ending with no hope beyond human effort; revenge pursued by sympathetic characters. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the gore and language are the depiction issue. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Concern for the outcast; consequences of evil; the body treated as something that matters.
frames.concerns: Adventist teaching on media (drawn from Ellen G. White and the church's guidelines) warns against entertainment that dwells on violence and horror; the cannibal premise also clashes with the health message. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Prejudice shown as wrong; peace preferred to violence.
frames.concerns: Witness publications (Watchtower, jw.org guidance on entertainment) counsel avoiding media that features violence (Psalm 11:5); fighting is the main way the story's conflicts are settled, though it is framed as tragedy, and the horror imagery is a heavy depiction concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Compassion and the hope of reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Christian Science teaching stresses spiritual reality over material sense, so media that dwells on bodily horror, disease and death runs against the habit of thought it encourages. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Strong critique of prejudice and state violence against a minority; empathy for the marginalized; Ishida's majority/minority framing.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; little agency for some female characters; mental-health portrayal needs care.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; memory of the dead; revenge shown as a cycle that destroys (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Eating human flesh and blood breaks food and purity law in its deepest form, though the story frames it as horror. Lashon hara and nivul peh make the language a concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; revenge rejected by the story's outcome.
frames.concerns: No turn toward repair at the end. Degrading content and vulgar speech are weighed by values of dignity; the cannibal premise is jarring for families who keep kosher.

frames.aligns: A plea against dehumanizing a minority, close to the prophetic call to justice; empathy for the hunted; cruelty shown as cruelty.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; few women with full arcs. Cruelty and exploitation are the ethical tests for the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; mercy; patience under suffering (sabr).
frames.concerns: Revenge pursued by sympathetic characters; no turn to God or mercy beyond human effort; the premise breaks the deepest taboo, eating human flesh, which the Qur'an (49:12) uses as the image of backbiting, though the story frames it as horror. Foul language and graphic violence are a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Dharma under impossible duties; karma of violence returning on all sides.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa and vegetarian traditions find the premise especially repellent; despair at the end.

frames.aligns: Craving (hunger) as the root of suffering; compassion for all beings; cycles of harm.
frames.concerns: First precept: killing is central; no liberation shown.

frames.aligns: Harmony and the hope of coexistence.
frames.concerns: Blood, death and corpses are kegare (impurity), so a story built on them weighs as depiction; no shrines or kami are mocked, which is this tradition's main concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Equality of all people; standing against injustice (the sant-sipahi ideal); service.
frames.concerns: Violence for revenge rather than defense of the oppressed; Sikh codes forbid intoxicants and many Sikhs avoid meat, so the premise is jarring. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The oneness of humanity and coexistence of opposed groups is the series' hope.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í writings counsel avoiding backbiting and degrading influences; heavy violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Scientology opposes psychiatry and psychiatric drugs; Kanou's surgical experiments and the CCG's medicalized control are framed as horrors, which fits concerns it raises, though the series' trauma framing differs. "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness) and glorified violence in places. No public Scientology guidance on manga found. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for nature and for beings unlike us; balance.
frames.concerns: The Wiccan Rede "an it harm none" is broken by every faction; revenge. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of prejudice against a minority and of state violence; empathy for the hunted; Ishida's majority/minority statement.
frames.concerns: Few women with full arcs; Tsukiyama's coding mixes queer and predatory traits; safe-messaging concerns about self-harm and suicidal thinking.

frames.aligns: Reason, empathy and the value of a finite human life; refusal of easy good and evil.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting; mental-health portrayal without support or recovery; bleak ending.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, protecting friends, a café that keeps order and restraint.
frames.concerns: Anti-authority strand (the CCG as oppressor); violence, language and moral grayness; no clear heroes.

frames.aligns: The Satanic Temple's tenets of compassion and justice, and the Church of Satan's focus on the individual, fit the story's sympathy for the outcast and its critique of the herd. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Cruelty and non-consensual harm conflict with TST's tenets on bodily autonomy.

frames.aligns: First Principle, the inherent worth and dignity of every person, extended to the "other"; justice and compassion.
frames.concerns: Violence and despair; no community repair at the end. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge spreads harm: Mado's zeal and Touka's attacks (ch. 13-29) and Yamori repeating his own abuse (ch. 59-66). Kaneki's hardening to protect friends brings him no peace (ch. 80-94).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Authority on both sides, the CCG and Aogiri, uses violence as policy and is critiqued. Anteiku's quiet restraint, outside both systems, is the endorsed path.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family and protecting one's group come first (Anteiku, the Kirishima siblings, Hinami). Hide's friendship regardless of what Kaneki is, and the hope of coexistence, widen the circle.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A hidden minority hunted by an organized majority; prejudice and state violence are critiqued. Aogiri's "strong eat the weak" creed is shown as hollow.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christian imagery recurs ("Original Sin," ch. 126; the church fight, vol. 4-5) but is symbolic and offers no rescue. Kanou's lab science is shown as horror (ch. 95-111), so neither pole is celebrated.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates a world of constant death, but the story's central value is tolerance across groups and the choice of one's own identity (life message).

folkways.japan: Ishida's sense of being "between the majority and minority groups" speaks to conformity pressure in Japanese society; Kaneki's mother's ethic, "better to be hurt than to hurt others," echoes Japanese ideals of self-effacement that the story tests and then breaks.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Critical theory, Might makes right (critiqued), Communitarianism, Nihilism (explored).

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The ruin of a proud man who makes himself judge of life and death; the innocent suffer from his "justice"; lawful authority prevails. Evil is shown in order to be understood, not made finally attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace; the "Mu" rule denies judgment and afterlife; Light's glamor can invite admiration. Coerced suicides and death gods weigh as depiction; many parishes would treat it as older-teen reading.

frames.aligns: Light as a picture of the passions, above all pride, and of a man refusing repentance; an Orthodox writer at Geeks Under Grace reads it as "the throne without the Cross."
frames.concerns: No hope of resurrection in the story's rules; death gods taken seriously as spirits; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the long dwelling with a killer's mind.

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin (Galatians 6:7); deception exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: A human claiming divinity is punished, but no gospel answer is given; the "Mu" ending; death gods. Profanity in the Viz text and coerced suicide fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the "compelling plot" and "conversations on morality and justice"; Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne and falling.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of "spiritual themes, violence, and language" and apple and Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

frames.aligns: The man who takes a death god's power is destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a supernatural death god who gives a human power to kill, and a notebook that works like a curse, are shown without any power of God against them.

frames.aligns: Light as a study in total depravity: a gifted, "good" student whose heart turns to self-worship; through common grace, a non-Christian story tells the truth about sin and the magistrate's sword.
frames.concerns: No grace or providence named; constant lying by the protagonist; coerced suicides (self-murder, WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: God works through lawful authority (police, courts), and Light usurps it; the law exposes him in the end.
frames.concerns: The story shows law and judgment but no gospel. LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: "Do no harm" set against a man who does harm for "good"; Soichiro's integrity.
frames.concerns: Light refuses every chance to turn back, and the story offers none; profanity; holiness churches stricter than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Moral crime fiction in the Sayers tradition, judged by how it frames good and evil; lawful authority (Article 37) frames the duel.
frames.concerns: The nihilist "Mu" close; Light's glamor. ACNA families may be more cautious than Episcopal families.

frames.aligns: Violence and the will to punish shown as a trap that consumes the one who uses it; a critique of the death penalty.
frames.concerns: The heroes also use deception, confinement and guns; no peaceful alternative is shown. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families may read it as a critique of capital punishment.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; honesty (Article of Faith 13) as what finally defeats a liar.
frames.concerns: The "Mu" rule against the plan of salvation; no repentance. Coerced suicide, profanity and the body count weigh against media that invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Pride and self-made godhood brought to ruin; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: Death gods and a spirit realm (spiritualism is strongly rejected); the "Mu" rule shares the teaching that the dead are unconscious but denies resurrection. Ellen White's caution about fiction that excites the passions. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Human attempts to rule and judge end in ruin; no hellfire (Ryuk: "no heaven or hell").
frames.concerns: Death gods as real spirits granting power (spiritism, a major concern in jw.org counsel); death as final with no resurrection hope; violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Truth exposes error; the deceiver's power proves empty.
frames.concerns: Death presented as real and final, against the teaching that life is spiritual; long dwelling on fear and death as mental influences. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of the death penalty, vigilantism, surveillance and populist media fits the peace-and-justice focus.
frames.concerns: Women defined by love for Light (AnimeFeminist); suicides without mental-health framing.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and due process; the danger of a man who makes himself an idol, brought down.
frames.concerns: Taking life outside lawful courts is never redeemed; a human claiming godhood. Coerced suicide and death gods; Haredi homes would avoid it. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Due process; the idolatry of power exposed.
frames.concerns: Suicide (traditionally forbidden); the "Mu" ending. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ethical monotheism's warning against self-deification; critique of vigilante justice and surveillance.
frames.concerns: Flat women; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unjust killing is grave and arrogance (kibr) leads to ruin; a human calling himself god (shirk) is destroyed.
frames.concerns: The story ends by denying the afterlife and divine judgment ("Mu"); suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Karma-like return: Light's actions bring his own end; satya (truth) defeats deception.
frames.concerns: Ego (ahamkara) never overcome; ahimsa; respect for parents broken.

frames.aligns: Karma-like logic; attachment to power and self drives suffering; Ryuk's detachment echoes impermanence.
frames.concerns: Constant false speech and killing (first and fourth precepts); the "Mu" ending can read as nihilism rather than Buddhist emptiness, though "mu" is also a Zen term.

frames.aligns: Death gods are folk figures, not kami; impurity and disorder end in ruin; sincerity (makoto) defeats deceit.
frames.concerns: Death and corpses (kegare) as constant imagery. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) shown as the root of ruin; justice belongs to God, not to a self-made judge.
frames.concerns: Ego, anger and pride shown at length in an attractive lead; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Justice requires lawful institutions; the would-be judge falls.
frames.concerns: No spiritual hope; violence against the commitment to non-violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: "Do not murder" upheld by the plot; "be worthy of trust" set against Light's lies.
frames.concerns: Death as final nothingness contradicts the teaching of the immortal thetan. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The threefold-return idea that harm comes back to the one who does it; death figures shown as folklore.
frames.concerns: Death gods as mere tools of harm. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of vigilante "justice," the death penalty, mass surveillance and populist media.
frames.concerns: Flat female characters (AnimeFeminist); suicides without safe-messaging framing; police torture-like methods shown as clever; no LGBTQ+ characters (CSM).

frames.aligns: Reason, evidence and due process win; human life defended without religious grounding; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: The glamor of a clever killer.

frames.aligns: Law and order matter; the police and a good father (Soichiro) are honorable; evil is defeated in the end.
frames.concerns: The glamor of a teen killer; the story's ambiguity about justice; Light deceives his father.

frames.aligns: A warning against anyone who makes himself god over others and against blind followers (the Kira cult).
frames.concerns: Church of Satan teaching accepts harsh retribution, so some may sympathize with Light's goal; The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and justice fit the critique. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Worth of every person, including criminals; justice through fair process.
frames.concerns: Flat women; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Private judgment and killing are the story's target: Light's vigilante "justice" ends in exposure and death (ch. 103-107). Soichiro and the task force, who stand for rule of law, duty and honesty, are the moral center.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Law and due process are endorsed over one man's will. L's surveillance and confinement of suspects (Misa, ch. 33-35) are questioned, so order is honored but not without limits.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rules are meant to apply to all, including family: Soichiro serves the investigation even as it points at his son. Light risks his father and sister (vols. 7-9), a betrayal of kin the story condemns as part of his corruption.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light's claim to be "god of the new world" (ch. 1-2) is the root wrong; no person is above the law. The police chain of command and the Wammy's House succession (Near, Mello) are shown neutrally.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious language belongs to the villain and his cult (Mikami, ch. 83; the Kira worshippers, ch. 108). The "Mu" rule offers a naturalist note, and the duel is won by reason and investigation.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Crime, safety and deterrence are the central question; a frightened public accepts a killer who promises security (Pragmatic lens). Ohba's takeaway, "let's give it our all while we're alive," adds a modest self-expression note.

folkways.japan: Capital punishment, a powerful police bureaucracy and the public's quiet approval of Kira reflect debates in Japan, which keeps the death penalty; scholar Jolyon Baraka Thomas reads the cult elements against the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack. Soichiro's quiet devotion to duty echoes Japanese workplace norms.

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored, mostly as imagery and structure), Existentialism (explored).

entry.heading: Black Clover
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned by effort, not birth: you refuse to give up, you lift up the people others look down on, and you build a family out of misfits.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the poor and the orphan; a church that shelters children; evil (the Dark Triad, Lucius) is never made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7); reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero's power comes from a devil shown as a friend; angels and "holy war" imagery belong to the villain; a consecrated nun is the object of a running marriage-proposal gag.

frames.aligns: Humility and endurance; love for enemies; a church that raises orphans.
frames.concerns: Demons are real in the tradition, so a demon made sympathetic and fused with the hero (Devil Union, ch. 272-273, 326-327) blurs the line; angelic forms (halos, wings) given to the villain's creations. Guarding the senses (nepsis) applies to the steady combat.

frames.aligns: Hard work, perseverance, care for the outcast (James 2:1-9 on favoritism to the rich).
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as the hero's tools; views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; underdog grace; forgiveness of former enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero befriends and unites with a devil; spiritual realities in the story are not Christian ones. Engage-or-separate views differ.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance and a church shown kindly.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": devil contracts and hosting are the main source of power for heroes and villains alike, and the hero's union with a devil is celebrated (ch. 270, 326-327). Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians; human pride and lust for power (Lucius, the Dark Triad) shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Devil alliance as the hero's strength; WLC Q139 concern for the fan service; images of angels and "holy war."

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Magic Knights bear the sword to protect the weak; vocation and faithful service in ordinary roles.
frames.concerns: Devil power and magic; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: lifting up the poor and the excluded; works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in former enemies who turn.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules caution about diversions; the devil alliance; drinking played for laughs. Holiness churches usually more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil, in a fantasy tradition (Lewis; Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings is among Tabata's named influences, per Wikipedia); justice for the excluded.
frames.concerns: The devil alliance and inverted angel imagery; the nun gag. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Care for outsiders, community of misfits, forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Heroic violence is the hero's main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and effort; family (including adoptive family); service in a squad.
frames.concerns: Devil power and occult-style magic; fan service and drinking. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Strong critique of class, birth and ethnic prejudice; the excluded become heroes; a church that shelters children.
frames.concerns: The nun gag and early thin female cast (Anime Feminist; Fandom); violence as the means.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, care for orphans, clear defeat of devils.
frames.concerns: Magic, witches and devil hosting throughout; the dead brought back as Paladins conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Kindness to the poor, loyalty, hard work.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic are the basis of the whole world, and the hero's power comes from a demon (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting is the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Persistence, hope and love outlasting hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, devils and fear are shown as real powers; magic as the source of strength.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan and stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18-19); honoring those who raised you; persistence.
frames.concerns: Magic (kishuf) and demon alliances are central; Kabbalistic terms (Qliphoth, Sephira) used as fantasy labels; tzniut concerns with outfits and gags. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Love of the stranger, social justice, reconciliation after historic wrong (the elves).
frames.concerns: Magic and demons; Kabbalistic terms as fantasy; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: dismantling prejudice by birth and nation; outsiders included; historic injustice remembered and repaired.
frames.concerns: Kabbalistic terms used loosely; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor, the orphan and the stranger; patience (sabr) and effort; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Magic (sihr) is central; the hero allies with a devil (shaytan) and fuses with it; angelic imagery used by the villain. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for outfits and gags.

frames.aligns: Effort and duty; a warrior who fights without hatred; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the fighting; the birth-and-rank hierarchy story invites discussion that families approach in different ways.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts and former enemies; Licht's hatred shown as suffering; craving for power (Lucius, Dark Triad) leads to ruin.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the main solution, against the first precept; ambition for the top rank is celebrated.

frames.aligns: Rejection of caste and birth-rank is a core Sikh value; courage to defend the oppressed; the five vices (ego, anger, greed) in the villains are condemned.
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as a fantasy device; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Elimination of prejudice of every kind (race, class, nation) and the unity of peoples, as elves, humans and kingdoms are reconciled.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting; drinking played for laughs (alcohol is forbidden to Bahá'ís).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; the Hino Country and the Ryuzen clan draw on Japanese setting.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; devils are a Western-style underworld rather than kami or yokai.

frames.aligns: Magic as part of nature; spirits of the elements (Undine, Sylph) aid the heroes; Vanessa, a witch, is a sympathetic hero.
frames.concerns: The Witch Queen is a manipulative ruler (likely ch. 90s; to verify); a stereotype check for "witch" villains.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be industrious, do not murder; self-determinism in Asta.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; Lucius rewriting souls and minds is condemned, which fits the Church's concern about mind control.

frames.aligns: Anti-discrimination by class, ethnicity and ability is the core theme; disability-like "no magic" hero succeeds.
frames.concerns: The Sister Lily gag (Anime Feminist: a "refusal to respect a woman's wishes"; Fandom: "a kind of stalker"); fan service; Common Sense Media rates diverse representation "very little."

frames.aligns: Worth earned by effort and character, not birth or bloodline; human solidarity across peoples; magic read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main tool; revivals lessen the weight of death.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-reliance, loyalty, duty, protecting the weak, respect for good mentors and a legitimate elected leader.
frames.concerns: Inherited aristocracy is critiqued; blood family often fails while found family succeeds; some religious conservatives raise the devil alliance.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person regardless of birth or power; justice for the excluded; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Violence as the means; the nun gag.

frames.aligns: A devil reframed as a misunderstood outcast; defiance of unjust authority and false holiness (Lucius's "Archangels"); self-reliance; Satanic Temple tenets on compassion and justice.
frames.concerns: Most devils are still villains, so the stereotype check applies; loyalty and self-sacrifice for the group over the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Asta answers insults by proving himself, not by revenge; rivalry is a matter of pride, but vendetta (Licht's, the elves') is shown as manipulated and is reconciled (ch. 214).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The chaotic, rule-bending Black Bulls are celebrated (ANN: "the magical misfits"), but the Magic Knights and the elected Wizard King are upheld (ch. 392).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family over blood: an orphanage and a squad, while Noelle's blood family is cruel (ch. 5). Protecting the whole kingdom, and later former enemies, is the goal.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank by birth and magic is the main target (Noble, Common and Forsaken realms); merit, not lineage, earns rank. The story still celebrates reaching the top rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The church is warm, but faith does not guide the plot; inherited aristocracy is critiqued; magic works like a natural force.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance drive the hero (survival), joined to tolerance of outsiders and being oneself (expression).

folkways.japan: Senpai-style mentoring by captains, group loyalty to a squad and hard-work ("ganbaru") perseverance are common Japanese shonen norms. The church, nuns and the European-fantasy kingdom are borrowed Western settings, and the Hino Country (Yami's home) is a Japan-like land seen from outside.

entry.dominant: Progressivism (anti-discrimination), Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pagan / occult (as fantasy setting), Critical theory (class).

entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

frames.aligns: Love of enemies and redemption of villains (Gaara, Nagato, Obito); an outcast child's dignity; self-gift for friends; revenge shown as a trap.
frames.concerns: Voyeurism treated as a lovable quirk (Jiraiya); spirit summoning and reanimation, judged by framing; suicide in backstories (Sakumo).

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies and repentance of villains echo theosis; self-sacrifice for friends.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so a demon fox sealed in a child, spirit summoning, reanimated dead and a death-god cult read as more than fantasy for many families. Constant killing, which the tradition holds calls for repentance even in war; guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, a hero who refuses revenge (Romans 12:19). Grace-like acceptance of an outcast (Beneath the Tangles reads Iruka's acceptance through Ephesians 2).
frames.concerns: Spells, summoning and spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a peeping mentor shown as wise; Tsunade's drinking played for laughs, a concern for teetotal Baptists.

frames.aligns: Servant leadership, grace before merit, forgiveness of enemies (Beneath the Tangles). Many evangelicals accept Tolkien/Lewis-style fantasy magic.
frames.concerns: Chakra, summoning and reanimating the dead may read as spirit contact rather than Tolkien-style magic. Fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, and a hero who will not take revenge.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a demon-like beast sealed in a child, the Jashin blood ritual, spirit summoning and reanimation are often a strong concern even in fiction. Sexual gags and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work shows real goods such as sacrifice and forgiveness. Every main character is flawed, which fits total depravity; villains are not simply monsters.
frames.concerns: Occult imagery; a lascivious mentor (WLC Q139); Sakumo's suicide (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Naruto cannot earn acceptance by effort alone; it comes first from Iruka. Two kingdoms: rulers bear a sword and can abuse it (Danzo).
frames.concerns: Occult elements (usually adiaphora in fiction, with care); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace: an outcast is loved before he changes. Social holiness: clan discrimination and secret violence challenged. Strong peace theme.
frames.concerns: Tsunade's drinking (holiness churches ask members to abstain); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Deep roots in fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis); forgiveness, sacrifice, reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity; occult-flavored powers, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: The central claim, that revenge must end and enemies be understood, is close to nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Yet nearly every conflict is settled by combat, and fighting is heroic. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media and value separation from "the world."

frames.aligns: Family and sacrifice; forgiveness; respect for teachers; the ending's marriages and children.
frames.concerns: A peeping mentor shown as wise; alcohol played for laughs (Word of Wisdom); spirit contact.

Reanimated dead and spirits of the dead shown as real conflict with the teaching that the dead sleep (Fundamental Belief 26); drinking; Ellen White's caution about fiction. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ending the cycle of war; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: Spiritism (summoning, reanimation, a death-god cult) is a major concern in jw.org counsel; violence as the main action (Psalm 11:5); loyalty to a military village. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and understanding overcoming hatred; an outcast's true worth seen.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and despair as recurring mental imagery; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Social justice: criticism of war, clan discrimination, secret police and child soldiers; reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: Gender roles (women as healers and wives); the Killer Bee stereotype CSM flags; fat jokes; harassment humor (Jiraiya).

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers and parents (Exodus 20:12); breaking cycles of revenge (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit summoning (Deuteronomy 18); mocking speech (fat jokes) as lashon hara-like; nudity gags against tzniut. Haredi homes would avoid it; Modern Orthodox families are selective. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for life and teachers; the end of revenge.
frames.concerns: Spirit summoning; nudity gags; mocking speech. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the anti-war theme; empathy for the outsider.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes (Killer Bee); gender roles. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mercy, patience (sabr), care for orphans (Qur'an 93:9), keeping promises, forgiveness over revenge (42:40).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and gambling played for laughs (5:90); sihr and spirit summoning (2:102); Shinto deity names, which some read as shirk imagery. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the nudity gags a strong depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect, rebirth (Indra and Ashura), chakra as life energy, dharma as duty to community.
frames.concerns: Hindu names (Indra, asura, chakra) used loosely in a fighting story; some may see careless use of sacred terms.

frames.aligns: The "cycle of hatred" mirrors the teaching that hatred is not ended by hatred. Pain's six bodies are named for the six realms. Naruto's choice not to take revenge.
frames.concerns: Buddhist terms used as names of weapons and a villain's bodies; violence (first precept); intoxicants played for laughs (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Kami names, harmony of the village and reverence for ancestors (the stone faces of past Hokage).
frames.concerns: Kami names (Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi, Izanagi) used as weapon names, which some may see as careless; death and blood without purification. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Overcoming ego (haumai) and anger; forgiveness over revenge; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Lust played as comedy (Jiraiya); drinking and gambling. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity of nations and the end of war; overcoming prejudice between clans; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Degrading humor against a "chaste and holy life"; drinking and gambling (both forbidden); summoning. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Basically good beings capable of change; survival of the group; honoring teachers and parents.
frames.concerns: Orochimaru's human experiments shown as evil (fits); violence; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Nature energy (Sage Mode); bonds with animal spirits; harm ended through understanding.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting against "harm none"; Hidan's cult as the only explicit religion is a villain's. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: An outcast's dignity, empathy for enemies, criticism of war, secret police and clan discrimination.
frames.concerns: CSM flags sexism, fatphobia, disability clichés and the Killer Bee stereotype. Child soldiers as normal. Women end as wives and mothers (ch. 699-700). Harassment humor.

frames.aligns: Peace comes from people understanding each other, with no god intervening; reason and empathy defeat ideology (Pain, Madara).
frames.concerns: Destiny and bloodline (the reincarnation reveal) cut against self-made achievement.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty to community, respect for teachers and elders, courage, inherited "Will of Fire," marriage and children at the end.
frames.concerns: A "pervert" mentor shown as wise; drinking and gambling; a hero who defies superiors.

frames.aligns: An outcast who becomes his own master; secret authority (Danzo) exposed.
frames.concerns: The story's central rejection of revenge cuts against Church of Satan teaching on retaliation; The Satanic Temple's compassion tenets fit better. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast; justice and peace; understanding across difference.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes and gender roles CSM flags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The cycle of revenge is the central problem; Naruto refuses revenge on Pain (ch. 443-453) and refuses to kill Sasuke (ch. 694-699). Winning recognition through effort and keeping one's word are still honored.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Loyalty to the village, respect for teachers and sacrifice for the community are presented as right (Socio-cultural lens). Secret authoritarian rule is critiqued (Danzo, ch. 481; the Uchiha massacre order, ch. 224-225).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The village comes before the clan: the Uchiha coup is the tragedy Itachi stops (vol. 43). Bloodlines still carry inherited powers, and the ending settles the cast into families (ch. 700).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Becoming Hokage is the dream (ch. 700); teachers and the Hokage line are honored, and ninja ranks structure life. Hidden heritage and bloodline decide much of the outcome (Pragmatic lens).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Shinto deity names and Buddhist ideas (the Sage of Six Paths, ch. 671; reincarnated souls) shape the world, though no one prays. The ending shifts toward destiny and myth (Shifts).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and sacrifice for the village dominate Part II. Naruto's drive to be acknowledged, and the peace he wins, give some place to self-expression.

folkways.japan: Group loyalty, respect for teachers (sensei and senpai-kohai bonds), duty to the village and the conservative gender roles of the ending reflect postwar Japanese norms; Kishimoto's "war is never the right answer," credited to his grandfather, reflects Japan's postwar pacifism.

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (village and "Will of Fire"), Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named. Wikipedia's Naruto article notes Confucian values (respect for teachers, filial duty, group over self); the other labels are this entry's own.
